entry.title: SAP AI Core — A Step-by-Step SAP AI Core Integration and Deployment.
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP AI Core provides many capabilities, but in real projects we usually need one thing first: a reliable way to call an LLM from business automation.

In a recent customer project, we were tasked with automating an inbound logistics inbox where vendors sent shipping notices, updates, and cancellations in completely unstructured emails. Building and maintaining regex-based parser pipelines proved unsustainable because every vendor used different wording.

In this blog, I focus on a practical scenario: converting unstructured email content into structured JSON and using that output in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA). Instead of covering every SAP AI Core screen in detail, this post shows the minimum platform steps required to go from model setup to working API consumption.

Why This Scenario Matters

In business processes, incoming emails often follow inconsistent formats. Rule-based parsing becomes difficult to maintain when templates, wording, and structure keep changing.

Using an LLM through SAP AI Core allows semantic extraction of key fields such as sender, invoice number, amount, and approval status, and returns a consistent JSON output for downstream processing.

Where Workspace and Generative AI Hub Fit

To keep the process clear:

  • Workspace is the project boundary where your AI assets and runtime context are managed.
  • Generative AI Hub is where you select and test foundation models.
  • ML Operations is where you configure and deploy models as callable endpoints.
  • Administration supports secure setup such as secrets and resource isolation.
Prerequisites
  1. SAP AI Core subscription with access to foundation models.
  2. A deployed or deployable model executable in your environment.
  3. SAP Build Process Automation tenant with automation authoring permissions.
  4. Destination and authentication setup for secure API invocation.
Configuring and Deploying a Foundation Model in SAP AI Core

SAP AI Core provides a structured way to configure, deploy, and consume foundation models in enterprise applications. Once a model is deployed, SAP AI Core exposes an endpoint URL that can be used from your applications, including SAP Build Process Automation, CAP applications, and other custom services.

I will walk through the two key steps required to make a foundation model available for use:

  1. Configure the model
  2. Deploy the model

After deployment, you will receive a service URL that can be integrated into your application landscape.

Why This Matters
When working with Large Language Models in enterprise scenarios, it is not enough to simply select a model. You also need a governed runtime where the model can be configured, deployed, and consumed securely. SAP AI Core provides that operational layer.

Step 1: Create a Configuration

The first step is to create a configuration for the foundation model you want to use.

Enter Details
While creating the configuration, provide the following details:

FieldValue
Configuration Name<Name>
ScenarioFoundation Model
Version0.0.1
Executableazure-openai

After entering these values, click Next

Input Parameters

In the next step, provide the required input parameters:

  • Model Name
  • Model Version

These parameters define the exact model you want to work with. Once you have entered the values, verify them and click Next.

Review and Create


In the review step:

  • validate all the details you have entered
  • ensure the executable and model information are correct
  • click Create

At this point, the configuration is created successfully.

 

step 2: Create a Deployment.


Once the configuration is created, the next step is deployment.

After configuration creation, you will see a Deployment button. Click Create Deployment.

Select the Executable

Choose the executable that you selected during configuration creation.

Select the Configuration

Next, select the configuration that you created in the earlier step, then click Next

Choose Duration

For the duration or deployment type, select:

  • Standard

Then proceed to the next step.

 

Review and Create

In the review screen:

  • verify the deployment details
  • confirm that the correct executable and configuration are selected
  • click Create

Deployment Status

The deployment process may take a little time. Once the status changes to Running, the model is ready to use.

After that:

  • open the deployment details
  • locate the generated URL
  • use this URL to consume the model from your application

This URL can be used in:

  • SAP Build Process Automation
  • CAP applications
  • custom integrations
  • backend services that need LLM access

Using the Deployment URL in Applications

The deployment URL is the entry point for your application to call the model hosted through SAP AI Core. Instead of directly connecting your application to a model provider, SAP AI Core acts as the managed layer between the application and the underlying foundation model.

For example, in BPA, this URL can be used to invoke the deployed LLM as part of an automation workflow.

Conclusion:

If your goal is enterprise-ready LLM integration, keep the blog focused on an end-to-end outcome rather than a full feature tour. SAP AI Core gives the governed runtime, and BPA gives operational automation. Together, they provide a scalable pattern for converting unstructured content into actionable business data.

Our main takeaway from this real-world implementation is that enterprise AI is as much about governance as it is about intelligence. Utilizing SAP AI Core instead of direct-to-vendor API endpoints kept our authentication keys secure within our SAP BTP landscape, gave us centralized , and ensured our data processing remained compliant with enterprise privacy guidelines.

For prompt design guidance, refer to this blog:
Prompt Management in SAP AI Core

For deployment steps, refer to this blog:
Deploying a Foundation Model in SAP AI Core and Using It in SAP Build Process Automation

entry.title: Deploying a Foundation Model in SAP AI Core and Using It in SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Introduction

In my previous blog post, I covered [what is SAP AI Core] and its core capabilities for enterprise AI. Now, the next logical step is to integrate an LLM model from SAP AI Core into your SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) projects.

The goal of this blog is to show you how to call SAP AI Core's LLM endpoints from within BPA, enabling you to use foundation models for intelligent text processing, data extraction, and semantic understanding within your automation workflows.

Real time Use Case: Email Content to JSON Extraction

Consider a common business scenario: You receive unstructured email content and need to extract key information (sender, invoice number, amount, approval status, etc.) and convert it into structured JSON for backend API calls.

The challenge is that email content varies widely. Templates differ, content formats change, and manually parsing every variation is not scalable.

Solution: Use an LLM to understand the email content semantically and extract the required fields into a consistent JSON structure. SAP AI Core makes this possible without maintaining rigid parsing rules.

Prerequisites

Before you can integrate SAP AI Core into BPA, ensure you have:

  • SAP AI Core Access
    An active SAP AI Core subscription with at least one foundation model deployed and running.
  • Destination Configuration
    A destination configured in SAP BPA pointing to your SAP AI Core instance. Refer to the [SAP Help documentation] for details on setting up destinations.
  • SAP Build Process Automation Access
    An active BPA subscription with permissions to create and edit automations.
Step 1: Prepare Your Prompt

Before calling the LLM, craft a clear prompt that describes the task. The prompt should:

- Define the input (e.g., "You will receive an email content")
- Specify the output format (e.g., "Return a JSON object with fields: sender, subject, invoice_number, amount, approval_status")
- Provide examples if needed

For detailed guidance on prompt engineering and best practices, refer to the [Prompt Management in SAP AI Core] blog post.

Example prompt:

Extract the following information from the email content and return it as JSON:

  • sender: email address of the sender
  • subject: email subject
  • invoice_number: invoice number if present
  • amount: invoice or order amount if present
  • approval_status: approved, pending, or rejected

Email content: {emailContent}

Return only valid JSON, no additional text.

Step 2: Call SAP AI Core from BPA

In your BPA automation, use the Rest Call Web Service activity to invoke the SAP AI Core LLM endpoint. Here is the request payload structure:

const data = {
    "messages": [{
        "content":PromptQuery,
        "role": "user"
    }],
    "temperature": 1
    
};
 
return {
    method: 'POST',

    url: "inference/deployments/<url-content>/chat/completions?api-version=latest",
    responseType: 'json',
    resolveBodyOnly: false,
    rejectUnauthorized: false,
    headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'AI-Resource-Group' : 'default'
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(data)
};

Understanding the Request Structure

Messages Array
The messages array contains the conversation. Each message has:

  • role: user for user input, assistant  for model responses
  • content: The actual prompt or user query

Temperature
The temperature  parameter controls the randomness of responses:

  • 0: Deterministic (best for structured extraction)
  • 1: Balanced (default)
    - Higher values: More creative responses

For email-to-JSON extraction, a lower temperature (0.3–0.5) is recommended for consistency.

Deployment URL
Replace <deployment-url> with the actual URL obtained when you deployed your foundation model in SAP AI Core.

AI-Resource-Group
This header specifies which resource group the request should use (default is `"default"`).

Step 3: Process the Response

The response from SAP AI Core will contain the model's output. Extract the JSON from the response:

Example BPA step to process the response

let extractedData = response.choices[0].message.content;
let jsonData = JSON.parse(extractedData);

Now use jsonData.sender, jsonData.invoice_number, etc.

Real-World Example Flow

1. Email arrives → stored in a variable
2. Construct a prompt with the email content
3. Call SAP AI Core using Rest Call Web Service
4. Extract the JSON response
5. Validate the JSON structure
6. Use extracted fields to create a backend API payload
7. Call the backend system to process the data

Conclusion

Integrating SAP AI Core into your BPA processes unlocks powerful capabilities for handling unstructured data. Whether you are extracting information from emails, summarizing documents, classifying content, or performing semantic analysis, LLMs can simplify and automate complex logic that would otherwise require rigid rules or manual processing.

 

 
Integrating SAP AI Core into BPA gave our team a fundamentally different way to handle unstructured input. Instead of writing fragile parsing logic, we now  describe *what we want* in plain language via a prompt, and the LLM reliably delivers structured JSON in return.

If you have requirements to connect BPA with LLMs, this approach will significantly reduce development complexity and improve automation flexibility.

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 2: Feeding the Expert the Right Case File
entry.content:
Part 1 introduced the idea and the model. This post is about the unglamorous middle step everyone skips in the demo: getting the right data in the right shape in front of RPT.

Why the playground API, and not AI Core
This build calls RPT's public playground API, not a productive AI Core deployment. POC-tier constraint, not a design choice: there's no AI Core subscription behind this project. RPT-1.5 is now GA under AI Core, so a production version would likely start there instead.

Want to try the API yourself? The API overview page has a downloadable Postman collection. The token itself (RPT_API_TOKEN below) comes from rpt.cloud.sap/settings.

Parameters used in the request:

  • rows (required): array of data rows, each one an object keyed by column name. Comes straight from the Datasphere view below.
    • Context rows: complete rows, no [PREDICT] values, used as examples.
    • Query rows: rows containing [PREDICT] placeholders marking what needs forecasting.
  • index_column (optional): which column to use as the row identifier in the response. Set in the Python script.
  • scenario (optional): a free-text label for telemetry, max 100 characters. Does not affect the prediction itself. Set in the Python script.
  • explanations (optional): controls how much explainability data comes back. Set in the Python script.
    • explanations.top_column_scores (integer, 1–50, default 4): top feature-importance scores per query row.
    • explanations.top_relevant_context_rows (integer, 1–50, default 3): most relevant comparable row indices per query row.

Target columns and task type (classification vs. regression) aren't declared anywhere: they're auto-detected. Any column containing [PREDICT] in a query row is automatically treated as something to predict.

Where the data actually lives: SAP Datasphere
Datasphere sits in front of the source system as the governed layer: it's where "who's allowed to see this" and "what does this field actually mean" get decided once, centrally, instead of every downstream consumer making its own call. That governance is the actual reason it's in this architecture at all, not just a convenient place to park a SQL view.

A disclaimer worth stating clearly: all data shown or referenced anywhere in this POC is synthetic, proportionally inflated to preserve realistic patterns, and not traceable back to any real project or real spend.

Three views do the actual work, each built on the last:

  1. A graphical view, "Context Projects": takes the target project as an input parameter and selects all similar projects sharing a specific set of attributes with it.
  2. A second graphical view, "Context Data": calls "Context Projects" and calculates the actual historical spread percentage across the timeline for each one, based on that project's own milestones.
  3. A SQL view: unions the project being forecast (outcome columns nulled out) together with the 100 most recent comparable projects from "Context Data," including their real historical spread, ordered by project start date.
SELECT "ID",
       "[ATTRIBUTE 1]",
       ...
       "[ATTRIBUTE N]",
       NULL AS "Prior_FPE_",
       NULL AS "FPE_to_LPI_",
       NULL AS "LPI_to_LPLV_",
       NULL AS "LPLV_to_CSR_",
       NULL AS "Post_CSR_",
       100  AS "Total_Spend_"
FROM "Context_Data"(RESULT_STUDY : :RESULTSTUDY)
WHERE  "ID" = :RESULTSTUDY
UNION ALL
SELECT *
FROM   (
        SELECT   "ID",
                 "[ATTRIBUTE 1]",
                 ...
                 "[ATTRIBUTE N]",
                 "Prior_FPE_",
                 "FPE_to_LPI_",
                 "LPI_to_LPLV_",
                 "LPLV_to_CSR_",
                 "Post_CSR_",
                 100  AS "Total_Spend_"
        FROM "Context_Data"(RESULT_STUDY : :RESULTSTUDY)
        WHERE "[PROJECT_START]" <= :PROJECTSTART AND "ID" <> :RESULTSTUDY
        ORDER BY "[PROJECT_START]" DESC
        LIMIT 100
        )

The top half is just the one project being forecast, with its outcome blanked out. The bottom half is its 100 most recent comparables, and it only pulls ones that started before the target project, so nothing looks into the future. The target project also can't compare itself to itself. UNION ALL glues both halves into the one table RPT actually sees.

A finding worth flagging right here, since it hit this exact step: the SQL view above returns real NULLs for the query row's milestone columns, but RPT doesn't accept NULL; it expects the literal string "[PREDICT]" marking which fields need forecasting. The Datasphere OData API also paginates, so this substitution can only safely happen after every page has actually been collected:

for row in rows:
    for col in MILESTONE_COLS:
        if row.get(col) is None:
            row[col] = "[PREDICT]"

Access: the view is first exposed for OData consumption, and that OData request URL is what actually shows up in the Python code later in this post. Reaching it is done via OAuth2 Client Credentials: a service-to-service grant with no user in the loop, using an OAuth client configured with the purpose "Technical user."

Why Python, and not BTP-native JavaScript or CAP
Fair question, since BTP is already hosting this and consuming it downstream: why not build the whole thing in JS/CAP too, rather than bringing Python into a BTP-native stack?

Three reasons it stayed Python:

  • The data work is data-science shaped. Cleaning and typing comparable-project data is pandas' job. Rebuilding that in JavaScript would just reinvent a weaker version of it.
  • RPT is Python-first. Its SDK and nearly every example assume a Python caller.
  • FastAPI lets one backend serve three front doors (Joule, a browser widget, a scheduled job) without any of them caring that Python's behind it (more in a later post).

The pipeline, function by function
Authentication starts with an OAuth client of type "Technical user" created in Datasphere. From there, it's just the OAuth2 flow from earlier put into code: hit the token endpoint with that client's ID and secret, get a short-lived bearer token back.

def get_token():
    resp = requests.post(
        os.getenv("KAAR_DS_TOKEN_URL"),
        auth=HTTPBasicAuth(os.getenv("KAAR_DS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"),
                           os.getenv("KAAR_DS_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET")),
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()["access_token"]

Fetching the data hits the SQL view from earlier through Datasphere's OData API, passing in the target project and its start date. Since the API paginates, the function keeps looping on @odata.nextLink until there's nothing left to grab, then runs the placeholder swap and the two safety checks from before.

def fetch_rpt_ready_data(base_url, token, result_study, project_start="210012"):
    url = (f"{base_url}/api/v1/datasphere/consumption/relational/"
           f"CAPSTONE/Top_100_Context_Data/Top_100_Context_Data"
           f"(RESULTSTUDY='{result_study}',PROJECTSTART='{project_start}')/Set")
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}

    rows = []
    while url:
        resp = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
        rows.extend(data.get("value", []))
        url = data.get("@odata.nextLink")

    for row in rows:
        for col in MILESTONE_COLS:
            if row.get(col) is None:
                row[col] = "[PREDICT]"

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

PROJECTSTART is fixed for this POC deliberately, so every comparable project in the dataset gets considered rather than filtered out. Its actual purpose is backtesting: the same point-in-time filtering logic that powers a live prediction can also power a retrospective test run against real history, just by varying this one parameter. For a live production call, it would need to derive from the target project's own actual start date instead of being fixed.

Building the request is the smallest function in the chain, and mostly bookkeeping: turn the DataFrame into the list-of-records shape the API expects, and attach the index_column and explanations settings covered earlier.

def build_rpt_request(df, index_column="ID", scenario="Capstone",
                       top_column_scores=6, top_relevant_context_rows=5):
    return {
        "rows": df.to_dict(orient="records"),
        "index_column": index_column,
        "scenario": scenario,
        "explanations": {
            "top_column_scores": top_column_scores,
            "top_relevant_context_rows": top_relevant_context_rows,
        },
    }

Sending it is a plain POST with a Bearer token, no OAuth exchange this time, since the playground API takes a simple static token directly:

def call_rpt_predict(request_body, api_token):
    response = requests.post(
        "https://rpt.cloud.sap/api/predict",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_token}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json=request_body,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

That's the whole chain, end to end. Here's what it actually returns from a real call:

{
  "prediction": {
    "explanations": {
      "top_column_scores": [
        {
          "[ATTRIBUTE 7]": 0.112,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 8]": 0.168,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 3]": 0.287,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 9]": 0.26,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 10]": 0.173
        }
      ],
      "top_relevant_context_rows": [[28, 62, 19, 38, 18]]
    },
    "id": "40cb049e-74ce-449d-b164-daeac53b803f",
    "metadata": {
      "num_columns": 19,
      "num_predictions": 5,
      "num_query_rows": 1,
      "num_rows": 101
    },
    "predictions": [
      {
        "FPE_to_LPI_": [
          { "confidence": null, "confidence_interval": [4.1774, 74.7796], "prediction": 39.43674087524414 }
        ],
        "ID": "M0061234",
        "LPI_to_LPLV_": [
          { "confidence": null, "confidence_interval": [2.3416, 62.0136], "prediction": 35.535091400146484 }
        ],
        "LPLV_to_CSR_": [
          { "confidence": null, "confidence_interval": [0, 13.6526], "prediction": 5.464094161987305 }
        ],
        "Post_CSR_": [
          { "confidence": null, "confidence_interval": [0, 41.8149], "prediction": 17.41983985900879 }
        ],
        "Prior_FPE_": [
          { "confidence": null, "confidence_interval": [1.1257, 10.3671], "prediction": 4.337931156158447 }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "status": { "code": 0, "message": "ok" }
  },
  "delay": 326.6230847835541,
  "samplingMetadata": {
    "sampledFrom": 100,
    "sampledTo": 100,
    "strategy": "random",
    "downsampled": false
  }
}

num_rows: 101 and sampledFrom: 100 confirm the full context set actually made it into the call: the target project plus all 100 comparables, nothing dropped. Five predictions came back, one per milestone, each with its own confidence_interval. What every field in this response actually means, and what to do with it, is Part 3.

What's next

Part 3 picks up right where this response leaves off: what every field in it actually means, why the numbers don't sum cleanly, and how the explainability data gets reshaped for a human-readable narrative.

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 3: From JSON to a Trustworthy Sentence
entry.content:
Part 2 ended right where the RPT call returns. This post picks up with the actual response: what every field in it means, why the five numbers inside it don't add up to 100, and what it takes to turn that into something a planner would actually read.

Part 2 closed with a real response from a full 100-row context set, worth going through field by field here:

{
  "prediction": {
    "explanations": {
      "top_column_scores": [
        {
          "[ATTRIBUTE 7]": 0.112,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 8]": 0.168,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 3]": 0.287,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 9]": 0.26,
          "[ATTRIBUTE 10]": 0.173
        }
      ],
      "top_relevant_context_rows": [
        [
          28,
          62,
          19,
          38,
          18
        ]
      ]
    },
    "id": "9fbb2bcd-f9cb-44f6-a738-0eafc2041442",
    "metadata": {
      "num_columns": 19,
      "num_predictions": 5,
      "num_query_rows": 1,
      "num_rows": 101
    },
    "predictions": [
      {
        "FPE_to_LPI_": [
          {
            "confidence": null,
            "confidence_interval": [4.1774, 74.7796],
            "prediction": 39.43674087524414
          }
        ],
        "ID": "M0061254",
        "LPI_to_LPLV_": [
          {
            "confidence": null,
            "confidence_interval": [2.3416, 62.0136],
            "prediction": 35.535091400146484
          }
        ],
        "LPLV_to_CSR_": [
          {
            "confidence": null,
            "confidence_interval": [0, 13.6526],
            "prediction": 5.464094161987305
          }
        ],
        "Post_CSR_": [
          {
            "confidence": null,
            "confidence_interval": [0, 41.8149],
            "prediction": 17.41983985900879
          }
        ],
        "Prior_FPE_": [
          {
            "confidence": null,
            "confidence_interval": [1.1257, 10.3671],
            "prediction": 4.337931156158447
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "status": {
      "code": 0,
      "message": "ok"
    }
  },
  "delay": 253.52716398239136,
  "samplingMetadata": {
    "sampledFrom": 100,
    "sampledTo": 100,
    "strategy": "random",
    "downsampled": false
  }
}

The outer envelope: status, id, delay, samplingMetadata
These four live outside prediction and describe the call, not the forecast itself.

  • status: code: 0 / message: "ok" is the pipeline's first checkpoint. Anything else short-circuits before touching the actual numbers.
  • id: a UUID for this specific call, useful for tracing a single request through logs if something needs investigating later. Not used downstream in this build.
  • delay: how long the call took, in milliseconds. 253ms is fast for a call reasoning over 100 rows with no training step, a real example of "one call, one response, zero training" from Part 1.
  • samplingMetadata: confirms sampledFrom: 100 / sampledTo: 100 / downsampled: false: every context row sent actually got used; nothing was dropped for exceeding a limit.

metadata: a built-in sanity check

"metadata": {
  "num_columns": 19,
  "num_predictions": 5,
  "num_query_rows": 1,
  "num_rows": 101
}

Explanations: the part that makes this more than a black box
Two arrays live here, and both are indexed by query row, meaning if more than one project were being forecast in a single call, each would get its own entry. With one query row, there's one entry in each.

top_column_scores: relative importance of each attribute in producing this specific prediction:

{
  "[ATTRIBUTE 7]": 0.112,
  "[ATTRIBUTE 8]": 0.168,
  "[ATTRIBUTE 3]": 0.287,
  "[ATTRIBUTE 9]": 0.26,
  "[ATTRIBUTE 10]": 0.173
}

Only a handful of the 12 attributes show up- the ones RPT actually leaned on for this project- not a score for every column sent. That's real attribution: "this recommendation weighed [ATTRIBUTE 3] and [ATTRIBUTE 9] most heavily," not a guess dressed up as one.

top_relevant_context_rows: [28, 62, 19, 38, 18]. These are positional indices into the 100 context rows, not project IDs. Turning 28 into an actual project means holding onto the original row order and mapping the index back afterwards. Skip that, and the narrative layer has nothing but meaningless numbers to point to.

Predictions: five numbers, and the field that actually matters. Each milestone comes back with the same three-field shape:

{
  "confidence": null,
  "confidence_interval": [4.1774, 74.7796],
  "prediction": 39.43674087524414
}

confidence is consistently null for this kind of prediction, and it's not a fluke: confidence is a classification-style field (a probability for a predicted class), and this is regression, forecasting a percentage, not picking a category. confidence_interval is the regression equivalent, and it's what the human-in-the-loop trigger is built around instead.

Now the actual problem: these five numbers don't add up to 100

39.4367 + 35.5351 + 5.4641 + 17.4198 + 4.3379 = 102.1937

Real drift, about 2.19 points over. Each milestone was predicted independently, with no guarantee they'd sum cleanly, and this response proves they don't. For five slices of one fixed total, 102.19% isn't usable as-is.

The fix: look at interval width per milestone, the gap between low and high, since that's RPT's own signal of how unsure it was:

MilestoneIntervelWidth
FPE_to_LPI_4.18 – 74.7870.60 (widest)
LPI_to_LPLV_2.34 – 62.0159.67
Post_CSR_0 – 41.8141.81
LPLV_to_CSR_0 – 13.6513.65
Prior_FPE_1.13 – 10.379.24 (narrowest)

FPE_to_LPI_ has the widest interval by far, so instead of trusting its direct prediction (39.44), it is derived as a residual: 100 minus the other four.

100 − (4.3379 + 35.5351 + 5.4641 + 17.4198) = 100 − 62.7570 = 37.2430

37.24 versus the original 39.44, close to the 2.19 drift it needed to absorb. Not a coincidence: the residual absorbs exactly the slack the others left behind. Prior_FPE_, the narrowest interval, gets flagged separately as the most trustworthy part of the prediction. The logic stays conservative: whichever number RPT trusted least is the one that absorbs the correction, never the one that makes the total look tidy.

Here's the actual function behind that math; it's the same calculation walked through above, just generalised to run on any prediction response, not just this one example:

def rescale_to_100(prediction_row):
    milestone_cols = [k for k in prediction_row if k != "ID"]

    parsed = {}
    for m in milestone_cols:
        entry = prediction_row[m][0]
        lo, hi = entry["confidence_interval"]
        parsed[m] = {"prediction": entry["prediction"],
                     "width": hi - lo, "interval": [lo, hi]}

    residual_milestone = max(parsed, key=lambda m: parsed[m]["width"])
    most_confident_milestone = min(parsed, key=lambda m: parsed[m]["width"])

    others = {m: v["prediction"]
              for m, v in parsed.items() if m != residual_milestone}
    others_sum = sum(others.values())

    derived_value = 100 - others_sum
    escalate_bad_residual = derived_value < 0
    derived_value = max(derived_value, 0)

    final_percentages = {**others, residual_milestone: derived_value}

    return {
        "final_percentages": final_percentages,
        "derived_milestone": residual_milestone,
        "derived_milestone_raw_prediction": parsed[residual_milestone]["prediction"],
        "widest_interval": parsed[residual_milestone]["interval"],
        "most_confident_milestone": most_confident_milestone,
        "most_confident_interval": parsed[most_confident_milestone]["interval"],
        "escalate_bad_residual": escalate_bad_residual,
        "sum_check": sum(final_percentages.values()),
    }

escalate_bad_residual fires only when the derived value goes negative: the other four milestones already exceed 100% on their own. derived_value = max(derived_value, 0) keeps a flagged result non-negative but never silent; the actual mechanism behind the human-in-the-loop principle from Part 1. One narrow check for now; production would need more layered on top.

An open question worth putting out there: RPT predicts each of the five milestones independently, so nothing guarantees they sum to 100, and the rescale approach above is how this build handles that. It works, but I'd genuinely like to know if there's a cleaner or more native way to enforce a compositional constraint like this, one where a set of predictions has to logically add up to a fixed total, rather than deriving the least-trusted number as a residual after the fact. If you've solved this differently, or know of a standard pattern for it, I'd like to hear about it.

Getting the explainability data narrative-ready
Two small transformations happen before any of this reaches a language model:

  1. Row indices become project identifiers. top_relevant_context_rows comes back as [28, 62, 19, 38, 18], meaningless until mapped against the original context-row order, turning "index 28" into an actual project.
  2. Column scores become rankings, not raw numbers. "0.287" means nothing to a planner. What matters is which attributes mattered most, in order, in plain language, not a decimal score.

Intervals, though, get carried forward exactly as-is: [4.1774, 74.7796], never paraphrased as "highly uncertain": that tells a planner nothing actionable; "between 4% and 75%" does.

Pulling the explainability data out is a one-line extraction, since it's already sitting in the response for the single query row this build sends per call:

def extract_explanations(full_response):
    exp = full_response["prediction"]["explanations"]
    return {
        "top_column_scores": exp["top_column_scores"][0],
        "top_relevant_context_rows": exp["top_relevant_context_rows"][0],
    }

Building the actual prompt is where the RCTFC structure (Role, Context, Task, Format, Constraint) shows up directly as five labelled sections. A few things worth pointing out in the real version:

  • The prompt pulls the derived milestone's raw prediction and full interval straight from rescale_to_100, instructing the model to quote it rather than paraphrase.
  • escalation_block only gets added when escalate_bad_residual is true: flagged language doesn't exist in a normal-run prompt at all.
  • Comparable projects come from indexing back into the context DataFrame with top_relevant_context_rows, the same index-to-project mapping described earlier
def build_narrative_prompt(target_attributes, rescale_result, explanations, context_df):
    influential = [context_df.iloc[i].to_dict()
                   for i in explanations["top_relevant_context_rows"]]
    influential_summary = "\n".join(
        f"- {r['ID']}: [ATTRIBUTE 3]={r.get('[ATTRIBUTE 3]')}, [ATTRIBUTE 9]={r.get('[ATTRIBUTE 9]')}"
        for r in influential
    )

    factor_summary = ", ".join(
        f"{k} ({v:.2f})" for k, v in explanations["top_column_scores"].items()
    )

    spread_summary = ", ".join(
        f"{clean_milestone_name(m)}: {rescale_result['final_percentages'][m]:.1f}%"
        for m in MILESTONE_COLS
    )

    widest_lo, widest_hi = rescale_result["widest_interval"]
    confident_lo, confident_hi = rescale_result["most_confident_interval"]

    escalation_block = "" if not rescale_result["escalate_bad_residual"] else f"""
- IMPORTANT: This is a flagged, unusual case. The four milestones RPT
  was confident about already add up to {rescale_result['sum_check']:.1f}%
  on their own — more than the full 100% contract. Because of this, the
  {clean_milestone_name(rescale_result['derived_milestone'])} milestone
  had to be set to 0%, and the total does not actually add up to a valid
  100% plan. This result should NOT be used as-is and needs a human
  planner to review it before anything is finalized.
"""

    prompt = f"""
Role: You are a financial planning analyst explaining an AI-assisted
forecast to a program manager with no data science background.

Context:
- Target project: {target_attributes.get('ID')}, [ATTRIBUTE 3] {target_attributes.get('[ATTRIBUTE 3]')},
  [ATTRIBUTE 9]: {target_attributes.get('[ATTRIBUTE 9]')}
- Recommended spread across the 5 milestones: {spread_summary}
- One milestone ({clean_milestone_name(rescale_result['derived_milestone'])}) was NOT predicted directly —
  RPT's own estimate for it was {rescale_result['derived_milestone_raw_prediction']:.1f}%,
  with a plausible range of {widest_lo:.1f}% to {widest_hi:.1f}%, so it was
  instead calculated as the remaining balance after the other four milestones.
- RPT was most confident about {clean_milestone_name(rescale_result['most_confident_milestone'])}
  (plausible range: {confident_lo:.1f}% to {confident_hi:.1f}%).
- The factors that most influenced this prediction: {factor_summary}
- The most similar historical projects used as reference:
{influential_summary}
{escalation_block}
Task: Explain this recommended spread in plain English. Mention which
milestone was calculated rather than predicted directly, and why. Mention
which comparable projects most influenced the result.

Format: 4-5 sentences, no jargon, no bullet points, written for someone
who has never heard of a confidence interval.

Constraint: Do not state the spread is "correct" or "accurate" — describe
it as a recommendation grounded in similar historical projects. When
explaining why a milestone was calculated rather than predicted directly,
quote the exact plausible range given above — do not paraphrase it.
"""
    return prompt.strip()

Calling the model uses Gemini, not SAP's own Generative AI Hub. Same root cause as everywhere else in this series: no AI Core subscription behind this POC, and Generative AI Hub sits behind AI Core alongside RPT, so it wasn't reachable either, and Gemini's public API stood in instead. The client itself is created once, outside the function:

from google import genai
client = genai.Client(api_key=os.getenv("GEMINI_API_KEY"))

GEMINI_API_KEY is a personal key generated from a Google AI Studio account, not an SAP credential, and not something a production version of this build would keep using.

def generate_narrative(prompt, models=("gemini-3.5-flash", "gemini-3.5-flash-lite"),
                        max_retries=2, base_delay=2):
    last_error = None
    for model in models:
        for attempt in range(max_retries):
            try:
                response = client.models.generate_content(model=model, contents=prompt)
                return response.text
            except genai_errors.ServerError as e:
                last_error = e
                if e.code == 503:
                    time.sleep(base_delay * (2 ** attempt))
                else:
                    raise
    raise RuntimeError(f"All models exhausted after retries. Last error: {last_error}")

Here's what generate_narrative actually returns for the response walked through earlier in this post, masked the same way as everywhere else in this series:

For your upcoming project (M0061234) using [ATTRIBUTE 3], here's a recommended timeline spread grounded in historical data from our most similar past projects. This recommendation allocates 4.3% of the timeline to Prior FPE, 37.2% to FPE to LPI, 35.5% to LPI to LPLV, 5.5% to LPLV to CSR, and 17.4% to Post CSR. The forecasting tool was highly confident about the earliest phase, but its estimate for the FPE to LPI milestone had a plausible range of 4.2% to 74.8%, too wide a guess to trust directly, so we made it whatever the rest add up to. This outlook is grounded in similar historical projects sharing [ATTRIBUTE 3] with the target project: specifically M0058504, M0060708, and M0057214, as well as M0059110 and M0057212, drawn from two different [ATTRIBUTE 9] categories.

Worth noticing: it states the spread plainly, quotes the calculated milestone's exact range rather than paraphrasing it, names real comparables, and never calls the result "correct," just a recommendation grounded in comparable history, per the prompt's constraint.

What's next

Part 4 covers what it actually took to get this whole pipeline (the Datasphere connection, the RPT call, this narrative layer) running as a live, authenticated service on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, with enough detail for someone else to replicate it.

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 4: From Script to Service
entry.content:
Parts 2 and Part 3 built a pipeline that works when you run it by hand. This post is about the gap between "works when I run it" and "works as a service anything else can call," and exactly what that took on SAP BTP.

What "live" actually means here
By the end of Part 3, the whole chain (Datasphere query, RPT call, rescale, narrative) worked as a script. A script isn't a service. Nothing outside that script can reach it: not a Joule Skill, not a SAC widget, not a scheduled job. Turning it into something those things can reach meant wrapping it in an API and putting that API somewhere it stays reachable.

That "somewhere" is SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, a trial account for this build.

Two endpoints, and why only two
Exactly two FastAPI routes:

  • GET /health: unprotected by design. Publicly reachable for monitoring; no key needed.
  • GET /predict-spread/{study_id}: the pipeline, gated behind X-Api-Key. Takes a project ID, runs the full chain, returns a typed response.

Every consumer in Part 5 (Joule, the SAC widget, the nightly job) calls this same single endpoint. One door handle, three front doors.

The actual app.py
Everything from Parts 2 and 3 gets imported straight in, not reimplemented. app.py is a thin FastAPI wrapper around the same functions already walked through:

from ds_call import (
    get_token, fetch_rpt_ready_data, build_rpt_request, call_rpt_predict,
    rescale_to_100, extract_explanations, build_narrative_prompt,
    generate_narrative, MILESTONE_COLS, clean_milestone_name
)

class PredictSpreadResponse(BaseModel):
    study_id: str
    final_percentages: Dict[str, float]
    escalate: bool
    derived_milestone: str
    most_confident_milestone: str
    narrative: str

PredictSpreadResponse declares exactly what the endpoint returns: percentages, escalation flag, derived milestone, narrative, typed and named, not a loose dict.

  • Why it's mandatory for Joule: SAP Build imports its Action contract from the generated OpenAPI spec. No declared response model means no named response fields; the Action's Output tab comes up empty, with nothing for a Skill to map to.

Auth is a dependency, not an inline check:

def verify_api_key(x_api_key: str = Header(...)):
    if x_api_key != API_SECRET:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid or missing API key")

@app.get("/predict-spread/{study_id}", response_model=PredictSpreadResponse,
         dependencies=[Depends(verify_api_key)])
def predict_spread(study_id: str, project_start: str = "210012"):
    ...

Depends() runs verify_api_key before the route body executes: a bad key never reaches the pipeline. The code's own comment says why this is enough for now: a proportionate check for a POC, with SAP's XSUAA service as the real production answer instead of a shared secret.

CORS is configured, not left to defaults: the browser-based SAC widget in Part 5 enforces CORS, so the API has to explicitly allow it.

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_methods=["GET"],
    allow_headers=["X-Api-Key"],
)

The Final Call: Every function from the last two posts, called in sequence, percentages rounded for display

def predict_spread(study_id: str, project_start: str = "210012"):
    try:
        token = get_token()
        df = fetch_rpt_ready_data(base_url="https://kaartech-2.br10.hcs.cloud.sap",
                                   token=token, result_study=study_id,
                                   project_start=project_start)
        request_body = build_rpt_request(df)
        result = call_rpt_predict(request_body, api_token=os.getenv("RPT_API_TOKEN"))
        rescale_result = rescale_to_100(result["prediction"]["predictions"][0])
        explanations = extract_explanations(result)
        target_attributes = df[df["ID"] == study_id].iloc[0].to_dict()
        prompt = build_narrative_prompt(target_attributes, rescale_result, explanations, df)
        narrative = generate_narrative(prompt)

        return {
            "study_id": study_id,
            "final_percentages": {
                clean_milestone_name(m): round(rescale_result["final_percentages"][m], 1)
                for m in MILESTONE_COLS
            },
            "escalate": rescale_result["escalate_bad_residual"],
            "derived_milestone": clean_milestone_name(rescale_result["derived_milestone"]),
            "most_confident_milestone": clean_milestone_name(rescale_result["most_confident_milestone"]),
            "narrative": narrative,
        }
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))

Deploying it: the unglamorous part

manifest.yml

applications:
  - name: capstone-respread-api
    buildpacks:
      - python_buildpack
    memory: 256M
    routes:
      - route: capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com

Procfile

web: uvicorn app:app --host=0.0.0.0 --port=${PORT:-8080}

requirements.txt

fastapi
uvicorn
requests
pandas
python-dotenv
google-genai

FastAPI apps deploy to Cloud Foundry the same way most Python web services do: log in and target the right org/space, then a manifest declaring the app, a Procfile telling Cloud Foundry how to start it, and a requirements.txt, then a single cf push.

cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
cf target -o <your-org> -s <your-space>
cf push

Credentials never live in code. Datasphere credentials, the API key, the model key, all set with cf set-env, never committed. Locally, the same values sit in a .env file that never gets pushed.

Every environment variable this build actually needs, gathered in one place since they're scattered across earlier posts otherwise:

GEMINI_API_KEY=
KAAR_DS_TOKEN_URL=
KAAR_DS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=
KAAR_DS_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=
RPT_API_TOKEN=
WIDGET_API_SECRET=

Testing it once live is a Postman call: hit the actual route with the API key in the X-Api-Key header:

GET https://capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/predict-spread/M0061234

Then confirm the response matches what the same call produces locally. No separate test suite, no CI step running against the live endpoint; a manual Postman request against the real Cloud Foundry route is the actual verification this build relies on.

What's next

With the pipeline live and reachable, the actual question becomes: reachable by what, and how? Part 5 covers three different answers to that: a conversational Joule Skill, a one-click SAC widget, and a nightly notification that runs without anyone asking, all calling this exact same endpoint, each suited to a different moment a planner might actually need this.

entry.title: Bridging the Gap: SAP AI Core vs. Model Context Protocol (MCP) in SAP Build
entry.content:
As enterprise AI matures, developers and architects are constantly looking for the most efficient, secure, and scalable ways to connect Large Language Models (LLMs) to their business data.

If you are building low-code/no-code applications using SAP Build, you have likely run into two different schools of thought:

  1. The Native SAP Route: Leveraging SAP AI Core and SAP AI Launchpad (via the Generative AI Hub).
  2. The Open-Standard Route: Utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to orchestrate AI tools and data access.

At first glance, these two approaches might seem to compete. You might ask: "If I already have a robust MCP server acting as a secure gatekeeper for my data, why do I need SAP AI Core at all?"

Let’s dive into the architectural realities of both, how they handle governance, and how to choose the right path for your SAP Build projects.

The Contenders: What Do They Actually Do?

1. SAP AI Core & Launchpad: The Enterprise AI Backbone

SAP AI Core is SAP’s native infrastructure engine for running, scaling, and managing AI models within the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). Together with SAP AI Launchpad (the administrative control center), it provides the Generative AI Hub—a secure gateway to top-tier foundation models (like GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini) pre-configured with enterprise-grade data privacy.

2. MCP (Model Context Protocol): The Open-Standard Gatekeeper

Developed as an open standard, MCP allows developers to build secure, modular servers that expose specific data sources and tools to LLMs. Instead of giving an LLM free rein over your backend, an MCP server acts as a strict API proxy. The LLM can only interact with the exact schemas, tools, and databases that your MCP server explicitly exposes.

The Governance Showdown: Two Paths to the Same Goal

Both architectures place a massive emphasis on governance and security, but they approach it from different angles:

Feature MCP Servers (Open-Standard) SAP AI Core (Native BTP)
Control PointDeveloper-Defined: You write the code to explicitly expose only the tools and data schemas the LLM is allowed to touch.Platform-Defined: Built-in enterprise data masking, tenant isolation, and strict compliance policies (GDPR, SOC2).
MaintenanceSelf-Managed: Your team is responsible for hosting, scaling, securing, and auditing the MCP server infrastructure.SAP-Managed: SAP handles the infrastructure, security patching, scaling, and compliance certifications out of the box.
IntegrationCustom APIs: Requires exposing the MCP server securely to the internet and configuring custom API destinations in SAP Build.Native Destinations: Seamlessly integrates with SAP Build Apps and Process Automation via native BTP destinations and SSO.

Why You Might Not Need SAP AI Core (The Case for MCP)

If you are a hands-on developer or part of an agile team with strong infrastructure capabilities, MCP servers are incredibly powerful.

  • Absolute Granular Control: You act as the ultimate gatekeeper. The LLM cannot access a single byte of backend data unless your MCP server explicitly permits it.
  • Flexibility: You aren't locked into any specific cloud ecosystem. You can run your MCP servers locally, on AWS, Azure, or on-premise.
  • Rapid Prototyping: For custom developer workflows, local testing, and highly specialized tool-calling, MCP offers an elegant, lightweight developer experience.

Why Enterprise IT Prefers SAP AI Core (The Case for Native)

While MCP is brilliant for custom control, large-scale enterprises often face hurdles when managing dozens of self-hosted MCP servers. This is where SAP AI Core shines:

  1. Zero-Trust Data Privacy: The Generative AI Hub guarantees that your business data is never used to train public LLMs. It automatically handles data masking and encryption without you having to write a single line of security code.
  2. Unified Monitoring (AI Launchpad): If five different departments are building SAP Build apps, how do you track token usage, costs, and latency? SAP AI Launchpad gives IT administrators a single dashboard to monitor and budget all AI consumption across the entire enterprise.
  3. No Infrastructure Overhead: You don't have to worry about hosting, scaling GPUs, or maintaining uptime for your custom servers. SAP manages the entire lifecycle.

The Verdict: Which Should You Choose?

The choice between MCP and SAP AI Core isn't necessarily an "either/or" decision—it depends on your organizational strategy:

  • Choose MCP if you want maximum architectural flexibility, have the resources to host and secure your own middleware, and want absolute, code-level control over how your LLMs interact with your custom tools.
  • Choose SAP AI Core if you are building production-grade applications in SAP Build that require instant compliance, native BTP security, zero-maintenance infrastructure, and centralized cost monitoring.

The Hybrid Future: In many modern architectures, these technologies can even work together. You can use SAP AI Core to securely access foundation models via the Generative AI Hub, while using your custom MCP servers to safely expose specific, non-SAP legacy databases to those models.

What is your take? Are you leaning toward open-standard MCP servers for your AI integrations, or does the out-of-the-box compliance of SAP AI Core make it the winner for your SAP Build projects? Let’s discuss in the comments below!

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 5: Ask, Click, or Wait
entry.content:
Part 4 got the pipeline live behind one API. This post covers three different front doors onto that same backend: a conversational Joule Skill, an embedded SAC widget with real write-back, and a scheduled notification that runs without anyone asking at all.

One backend, several front doors
Nothing about the underlying intelligence changes depending on how it's reached. The whole stack from Parts 2 to 4 stays fixed: What differs across the three options below is purely how it's reached, not the engine behind it.

Option 1: Conversational, a Joule Skill
The experience: the pipeline exposed as a custom Joule Skill, a natural-language question, "What's the recommended spend spread for project X?", typed into Joule, answered with the AI-generated narrative in plain conversation. SAP's own documentation lists the surfaces as "SAP Build Work Zone, SAP S/4HANA, SAP SuccessFactors, and other Joule-enabled applications" (however, SAC isn't named there explicitly). No navigation, no dashboard, no separate tool to open.

The scenario this was actually built for: a planner mid-way through a SAC Planning input story, wanting a quick sanity check before committing numbers, asking Joule the same question above, getting the narrative back inline, and going straight back to planning. Not a report run separately, but a question answered mid-task. Whether that's actually achievable today is genuinely unclear: see the honest gap at the end of this section before assuming it works.

  1. Create a BTP Destination connecting Joule Studio to the deployed backend, secured with a static API key kept out of visible configuration.
    • In the BTP Cockpit, under Connectivity, select Destinations and click Create.
    • Fill in Name, Description, Proxy Type as Internet, Type as HTTP, and the backend's URL: https://capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com.
    • Set Authentication to No Authentication, a POC choice, but also a requirement: a custom header added any other way gets silently dropped otherwise. 
    • Under Additional Properties, add the key exactly as URL.headers.X-Api-Key: that specific naming is what BTP Destinations require for a custom header, or it's silently ignored.
    • Click Create, then Check Connection.
    • Expose it to SAP Build, a separate step from creating it: add sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled: true and sap.processautomation.enabled: true under Additional Properties, then in the SAP Build Lobby go to Control Tower → Destinations, Add, select the Destination, Next, and pick the Shared Environment the Skill will deploy to. (If that Environment doesn't exist yet: Control Tower → Environments → Add Environment, create a Shared environment; it has to exist before this step, not just before the final Skill deployment.)
  2. Import an Action from the backend's own auto-generated OpenAPI spec: this is what tells Joule what the backend can actually do.
    • It's an upload flow, not a URL-import flow: visit https://<your-app>/openapi.json in a browser first and save that file locally, then run it through the conversion script further down this post (the OpenAPI 3.1 → 3.0 fix): the next step needs the converted file, not just a link to the live spec.
    • In SAP Build, under the Connectors section, select Action and create a new connection of type API Specification, then upload the converted JSON file.
    • Check the Input and Output sections match what the backend actually expects and returns, then test the connection by passing a real API key and a real project ID as parameters, confirming the Action reaches the live endpoint before wiring anything downstream to it.
    • Release and publish the Action once the test succeeds: it isn't usable by a Skill until it's published.
  3. Wrap the Action in a Skill:
    • Create a new project of type Agent and Skill.
    • Create a new Skill with an appropriate name and description.
    • Under the skill’s settings, disable “Allow Joule to generate a response” and enable “Allow skill to be started directly by the user,” mapped so Joule’s own LLM displays the backend’s narrative verbatim rather than rewriting or re-summarizing it. Not a minor setting: rewriting it would undo every constraint built into the narrative prompt in Part 3, including the “quote the actual interval, don’t paraphrase it” rule.
    • Under Parameters, create a new skill input with an appropriate description: this is what lets Joule map a user’s natural-language project reference to the actual parameter the Action needs.
    • Add a Call Action node right after the skill trigger.
    • In the Call Action's properties, select the Destination Variable as the Destination exposed to SAP Build in step 1.
    • Map the skill input to the Action’s project_id input.
    • On the End step, explicitly map the Action’s outputs back to the skill’s outputs, a separate, easy-to-miss step from adding the Call Action node itself; skipping it means the skill runs the API call but never actually surfaces the result.
    • On a successful API call, show the narrative response as a message to the user. On failure, show an appropriate error message. 
    • Release, then Deploy: choose the target environment and click Upgrade, and match the destination binding to the Shared Environment’s own destination, since it isn’t automatically inherited from dev.

One honest gap, kept simple: this Skill is never invoked from SAC in this series, not tried, since Joule isn’t enabled in the SAC system this build has access to. SAP’s own docs list Work Zone, S/4HANA, and SuccessFactors as the surfaces Skills reach; SAC isn’t on that list, and nothing found anywhere (SAP docs or community blogs) shows a custom Skill being invoked from SAC. Doesn’t rule it out, but as of today, this option is documented as reaching Work Zone, S/4HANA, and SuccessFactors, not SAC.

One finding while generating the OpenAPI JSON for action: FastAPI generates OpenAPI 3.1 by default; SAP Build's Action importer expects 3.0. Relabeling the version in the FastAPI constructor doesn't fix it: 3.1 and 3.0 describe nullable fields differently, so the schema actually needs rewriting, not renaming:

import json

def convert_31_to_30(spec):
    """Converts an OpenAPI 3.1 spec (FastAPI's default) to 3.0 format."""
    spec = json.loads(json.dumps(spec))  # deep copy
    spec["openapi"] = "3.0.3"

    def fix_schema(schema):
        if isinstance(schema, dict):
            if isinstance(schema.get("type"), list) and "null" in schema["type"]:
                remaining = [t for t in schema["type"] if t != "null"]
                schema["type"] = remaining[0] if len(remaining) == 1 else remaining
                schema["nullable"] = True
            for v in schema.values():
                fix_schema(v)
        elif isinstance(schema, list):
            for item in schema:
                fix_schema(item)

    fix_schema(spec.get("components", {}).get("schemas", {}))
    fix_schema(spec.get("paths", {}))
    return spec


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("capstone_openapi.json") as f:
        spec = json.load(f)

    converted = convert_31_to_30(spec)

    with open("openapi_v30.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(converted, f, indent=2)

    print("Converted. New version:", converted["openapi"])

Security model: access is gated through SAP's Identity Authentication Service: a specific user group, with the Skill's environment restricted to that group. Anyone outside it gets a generic fallback response, not an error, so the restriction fails gracefully rather than leaking that the Skill exists at all.

 

Option 2: Embedded, a custom SAC widget
The experience: a planner opens a SAC story already filtered to a single project. A widget embedded in that story lets them trigger the prediction with one click: the recommended spread and its narrative explanation appear inline, no leaving SAC, no separate tool. A second action uses that spread to calculate the actual forecast, then writes the result into the plan, turning the AI's recommendation into real plan data other reports and stories can consume.

Building the widget
The widget is a SAC custom widget: a manifest declaring what it exposes to story script, and a web component implementing the actual behaviour. Here's the manifest file:

{
	"id": "com.capstone.rptbox",
	"version": "1.0.0",
	"name": "RPT Prediction",
	"description": "Calls the forecast re-spread API for a study",
	"newInstancePrefix": "RptBox",
	"icon": "",
	"vendor": "Capstone POC",
	"eula": "",
	"license": "",
	"webcomponents": [
		{
			"kind": "main",
			"tag": "com-capstone-rptbox",
			"url": "/main.js",
			"integrity": "",
			"ignoreIntegrity": true
		}
	],
	"properties": {
		"studyId": { "type": "string", "description": "Study to predict for", "default": "" },
		"narrative": { "type": "string", "description": "Plain-English explanation", "default": "" },
		"escalate": { "type": "boolean", "description": "Needs human review", "default": false },
		"derivedMilestone": { "type": "string", "description": "Milestone derived as residual", "default": "" },
		"mostConfidentMilestone": { "type": "string", "description": "Milestone with narrowest interval", "default": "" },
		"finalPercentages": { "type": "string", "description": "Percentages as JSON string", "default": "{}" },
		"status": { "type": "string", "description": "idle, loading, success or error", "default": "idle" },
		"lastError": { "type": "string", "description": "Error message if call failed", "default": "" }
	},
	"methods": {
		"setStudyId": { "description": "Sets the study to predict for.", "parameters": [{ "name": "newStudyId", "type": "string", "description": "The study ID" }] },
		"getStudyId": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the study ID." },
		"invokePrediction": { "description": "Calls the backend for the current study ID." },
		"getNarrative": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the narrative." },
		"getEscalate": { "returnType": "boolean", "description": "Returns whether review is needed." },
		"getDerivedMilestone": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the derived milestone." },
		"getMostConfidentMilestone": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the most confident milestone." },
		"getFinalPercentages": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns percentages as a JSON string." },
		"getStatus": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the current status." },
		"getLastError": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the last error message." }
	},
	"events": {
		"onPredictionComplete": { "description": "Called when the prediction succeeds." },
		"onPredictionError": { "description": "Called when the prediction fails." }
	}
}

Web component file:

(function () {
  let template = document.createElement("template");
  template.innerHTML = `
		<style>
		:host { display: block; font-family: sans-serif; }
		.wrap { padding: 12px; }
		.status { font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px; }
		.status.error { color: #d32f2f; }
		.narrative { white-space: pre-wrap; font-size: 13px; }
		</style>
		<div class="wrap">
			<div class="status" id="status"></div>
			<div class="narrative" id="narrative"></div>
		</div>
	`;

  class RptBox extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
      super();
      let shadowRoot = this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
      shadowRoot.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
      this._shadowRoot = shadowRoot;

      // Single internal source of truth for every property.
      // All getters/setters and invokePrediction read/write these directly —
      // never through the SAC-managed property layer — so nothing depends
      // on the framework's deferred batch/render cycle.
      this._state = {
        studyId: "", narrative: "", escalate: false, derivedMilestone: "",
        mostConfidentMilestone: "", finalPercentages: "{}", status: "idle", lastError: ""
      };
    }

    onCustomWidgetBeforeUpdate(changedProperties) {
      this._state = { ...this._state, ...changedProperties };
    }

    onCustomWidgetAfterUpdate(changedProperties) {
      this._render();
    }

    setStudyId(newStudyId) {
      this._state.studyId = newStudyId;
      this._render();
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("propertiesChanged", {
        detail: { properties: { studyId: newStudyId } }
      }));
    }

    getStudyId() {
      return this._state.studyId;
    }

    async invokePrediction() {
      const studyId = this._state.studyId;
      if (!studyId) {
        this._fail("No study ID set. Call setStudyId() before invokePrediction().");
        return;
      }

      this._push({ status: "loading", lastError: "" });

      const BASE_URL = "https://capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com";
      const API_KEY = "[REDACTED]";

      try {
        const response = await fetch(
          BASE_URL + "/predict-spread/" + encodeURIComponent(studyId),
          { headers: { "X-Api-Key": API_KEY } }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
          const body = await response.text();
          throw new Error("API returned " + response.status + ": " + body);
        }

        const data = await response.json();

        this._push({
          narrative: data.narrative,
          escalate: data.escalate,
          derivedMilestone: data.derived_milestone,
          mostConfidentMilestone: data.most_confident_milestone,
          finalPercentages: JSON.stringify(data.final_percentages),
          status: "success"
        });

        this.dispatchEvent(new Event("onPredictionComplete"));
      } catch (err) {
        this._fail(err.message);
      }
    }

    _fail(message) {
      this._push({ status: "error", lastError: message });
      this.dispatchEvent(new Event("onPredictionError"));
    }

    _push(props) {
      this._state = { ...this._state, ...props };
      this._render();
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("propertiesChanged", { detail: { properties: props } }));
    }

    getNarrative() { return this._state.narrative; }
    getEscalate() { return this._state.escalate; }
    getDerivedMilestone() { return this._state.derivedMilestone; }
    getMostConfidentMilestone() { return this._state.mostConfidentMilestone; }
    getFinalPercentages() { return this._state.finalPercentages; }
    getStatus() { return this._state.status; }
    getLastError() { return this._state.lastError; }

    _render() {
      const p = this._state;
      const statusEl = this._shadowRoot.getElementById("status");
      const narrativeEl = this._shadowRoot.getElementById("narrative");
      if (!statusEl || !narrativeEl) return;

      let header;
      if (p.status === "loading") {
        header = "Loading prediction...";
      } else if (p.status === "error") {
        header = "Error: " + (p.lastError || "");
      } else if (p.status === "success") {
        header = p.escalate ? "\u26A0 Needs review before submitting." : "\u2713 Ready to submit.";
      } else {
        header = "Ready. Study: " + (p.studyId || "(none set)");
      }

      statusEl.textContent = header;
      statusEl.className = "status" + (p.status === "error" ? " error" : "");
      narrativeEl.textContent = (p.status === "error") ? "" : (p.narrative || "");
    }
  }

  customElements.define("com-capstone-rptbox", RptBox);
})();
  • _state is the single source of truth. Every getter, setter, and invokePrediction read/write it directly, never through SAC's managed property layer.
  • The constructor builds a shadow DOM once, attaching the template's markup inside attachShadow({ mode: "open" }), keeps the widget's internal styling isolated from the rest of the story.
  • onCustomWidgetBeforeUpdate merges any externally-set properties (e.g. studyId bound to a filter elsewhere in the story) into _state, so there's still only one source of truth even when SAC pushes changes in from outside.
  • onCustomWidgetAfterUpdate just calls _render(): SAC's own update cycle triggers a redraw, but doesn't write to state directly.
  • setStudyId updates _state, redraws, and fires propertiesChanged, the same pattern _push() uses later, done manually here since it's a plain setter, not part of the async prediction flow.
  • invokePrediction guards against an empty studyId first, sets status to "loading", fetches the backend with the X-Api-Key header, and maps the response fields into _state on success, or routes to _fail() on any error, including a non-OK HTTP response.
  • _fail() is the one path both a missing studyId and a failed fetch funnel through: sets status to "error", stores the message, and fires onPredictionError.
  • _push() updates _state and fires propertiesChanged, so anything bound to these properties in the story picks up the change too.
  • _render() produces the "Needs review" vs. "Ready to submit" text, the actual mechanism behind the safeguard described further down.

One honest gap: the API key sits in plain text in the widget's client-side JavaScript, visible to anyone who opens dev tools, unlike a key sitting server-side. Fine for a POC, not for anything that ships. Production fix and why: covered in the final post on what changes for enterprise.

Writing the result back into the plan
This is where the widget stops being read-only. Once a prediction comes back from the backend, the widget's onPredictionComplete event fires, and the story script bound to that event pushes the five percentages into the actual planning table using SAC's setUserInput and submitData APIs.

The response comes back as a JSON string that has to be parsed and converted before it can be written anywhere:

var lists = percents.split('":');
var prior_fpe = lists[1].substring(0, lists[1].indexOf(","));
var fpe_lpi   = lists[2].substring(0, lists[2].indexOf(","));
var lpi_lplv  = lists[3].substring(0, lists[3].indexOf(","));
var lplv_csr  = lists[4].substring(0, lists[4].indexOf(","));
var post_csr  = lists[5].substring(0, lists[5].length - 1);

// The Spread measure in this model is stored as a decimal fraction (0.372), not a
// whole-number percent (37.2) — matches how the existing RateCard values are stored.
prior_fpe = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(prior_fpe) / 100));
fpe_lpi   = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(fpe_lpi)   / 100));
lpi_lplv  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(lpi_lplv)  / 100));
lplv_csr  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(lplv_csr)  / 100));
post_csr  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(post_csr)  / 100));

var prior_fpe_sel = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "Prior FPE" };
var fpe_lpi_sel   = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "FPE to LPI" };
var lpi_lplv_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "LPI to LPLV" };
var lplv_csr_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "LPLV to CSR" };
var post_csr_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "Post CSR" };

tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(prior_fpe_sel, prior_fpe);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(fpe_lpi_sel, fpe_lpi);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(lpi_lplv_sel, lpi_lplv);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(lplv_csr_sel, lplv_csr);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(post_csr_sel, post_csr);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().submitData();
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getDataSource().refreshData();

 

Option 3: Proactive, a scheduled notification
The experience: every night, any newly created project gets automatically evaluated. The responsible manager gets a notification the next morning with the status and narrative already waiting; no one has to remember to ask, and no one has to click anything to get it started.

This runs as a scheduled SAC Application, whose script fires in onInitialization event, reusing the exact same RptBox widget from Option 2 above rather than making a fresh HTTP call to the backend.

var new_proj = tbl_new_projects.getDataSource().getResultSet();
console.log(new_proj);
var pms = ArrayUtils.create(Type.string);
var proj_ids = ArrayUtils.create(Type.string);
var email_title = "";
var i = 0;
var j = 0;

// Getting the unique list of project managers
for (i = 0; i < new_proj.length; i++) {
    if (!pms.includes(new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id)) {
        pms.push(new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id);
    }
}

// Batch processing the project IDs for each project manager
for (j = 0; j < pms.length; j++) {
    proj_ids.splice(0);
    for (i = 0; i < new_proj.length; i++) {
        if (new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id === pms[j]) {
            proj_ids.push(new_proj[i]["StudyID"].id);
        }
    }

    // Passing a single project ID, since the backend SQL view and APIs are
    // designed to handle only one predict row at a time for this POC. In a
    // production scenario, rather than calling the RPT API in a loop, it's
    // best to update the API to accept multiple project IDs and predict
    // everything in one call, for each project manager.
    RPT_JOB.setStudyId(proj_ids[0]);
    RPT_JOB.invokePrediction();

    if (RPT_JOB.getStatus() === "success") {
        if (RPT_JOB.getEscalate()) {
            email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results - Manual Review required";
        } else {
            if (utils.submitPredictionData(RPT_JOB.getFinalPercentages())) {
                // Returns true if the prediction was applied successfully to the forecast.
                email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results";
            } else {
                email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results - Not applied to the forecast";
            }
        }

        Application.sendNotification({
            title: email_title,
            content: RPT_JOB.getNarrative(),
            receivers: [pms[j]],
            isSendEmail: true,
            isSendMobileNotification: true
        });
    }
}
  • Pulls the new-project list. tbl_new_projects.getDataSource().getResultSet() reads from a table already scoped to newly created projects; this script doesn't do that filtering itself.
  • Dedupes down to project managers. One unique list of PM IDs from however many new projects showed up overnight.
  • Groups projects per manager, then predicts in one call. For each PM, it collects every new project ID belonging to them, and calls the prediction API on proj_ids[]
  • Three-state email title. Escalated (needs review), applied cleanly, or applied but write-back failed, not just success/fail.
  • One notification, two channels. Email and mobile push in the same call, using the widget's getNarrative() directly, no separate composition step.

Worth being upfront about the scenario this fits. This approach was built for a simple case: each project manager gets one or two new projects at a time, not a flood. It works well there, but it's not the shape you'd want at real volume.

For a high-volume scenario, a different architecture makes more sense. Rather than a SAC script looping through predictions one project at a time, the trigger would move upstream to Datasphere: a process there would call the prediction pipeline and write the results directly into the SAC Planning model's tables, including an attribute marking whether each project is escalated or not. A Data Action in SAC would then apply the predicted percentages based on that escalation attribute, only pushing the clean, non-escalated results into the plan. The scheduled SAC Application's job shrinks down to just one thing at that point: sending an email with a PDF export summarizing what got forecast and what got escalated, rather than driving the whole prediction loop itself.

What's next

Part 6 covers what's next: how this pipeline could actually be backtested against real outcomes, and what would need to change to take it from proof of concept to something a real enterprise could run on.

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 6: From Proof of Concept to Production
entry.content:
Part 5 covered three different ways to reach this pipeline: a Joule Skill, an embedded SAC widget, and a scheduled notification. This is the last post in the series, and the question it has to answer honestly is: after five posts of building, does any of this actually prove the AI-driven approach beats the formula it's meant to replace?

How the backtest could actually work
For any past project, backtesting means setting PROJECTSTART to that project's own actual start date, the same point-in-time filtering already built into the pipeline, so the comparable pool only includes projects that existed before that date. Running the pipeline this way produces exactly what RPT would have predicted at the moment that project was actually being planned, not with the benefit of hindsight.

That prediction can then be compared against the historical average-formula spread that was actually used for that project at the time, provided that value is still recoverable somewhere: an archived report, a snapshotted export, a record kept outside the live system.

A second option, alongside backtesting against historical averages: run both approaches prospectively, side by side, in shadow mode. For new projects going forward, planners keep working exactly as they do today, with the current average-calculated spread still the number they see and use, while this pipeline's predictions get generated and logged alongside it, unseen and non-binding, purely for comparison. Over time, enough real outcomes accumulate on both sides to compare which one actually tracked closer, without ever putting an unproven number in front of a planner making a real decision.

What influenced this build
Two pieces of outside evidence shaped real decisions in this series, not just retrospective validation found after the fact:

  • On the technology choice itself: an independent benchmark tested SAP-RPT against classical models (LightGBM, CatBoost) across 17 datasets. Classical models won most categories, but SAP-RPT came out ahead specifically on small, data-scarce datasets, exactly the situation this build is in: a limited pool of genuinely comparable historical projects, not a massive dataset. That's part of why RPT was the right fit here rather than a classical model. (Source) SAP's own Sapphire 2026 announcement of SAP-RPT-1.5 reinforces the same design instinct this series leaned on: its new explainability enhancements are described as delivering "explanations at the column and row levels, helping users identify the business attributes and historical records that influenced predictions," the same idea behind this build's own top_column_scores and top_relevant_context_rows handling in Part 3. (Source)
  • On the human-in-the-loop design: SAP's own Global AI Ethics policy states human oversight as a core principle, requiring that automated decision processes allow for human intervention. The escalation-trigger design this series has leaned on since Part 1 follows that same principle directly: it's not a nice-to-have layered on top; it's the actual mechanism that makes an AI-derived number safe to act on.

What changes between this POC and something enterprise-ready
Every trial-tier system in this build (AI Core, BTP, Datasphere) moves to its enterprise equivalent. 

Auth changes at several different layers:

  • Backend API access — the shared static X-Api-Key checked in app.py gets replaced with real per-consumer credentials via SAP's XSUAA service, not a single key everyone shares.
  • The SAC widget specifically — right now the API key sits in plain text in the widget's client-side JavaScript, visible to anyone who opens dev tools. This needs proper OAuth through XSUAA at the widget layer, not a key baked into the bundle.
  • The RPT connection — the playground's simple Bearer token gets replaced with AI Core's own service-key-based OAuth once that subscription is in place.
  • The Datasphere connection — already uses OAuth2 Client Credentials with a Technical User client, which is the correct enterprise pattern; this one's closer to production-ready than the others already, mainly needs the trial-tier constraints lifted.
  • The narrative-layer LLM connection — a personal API key gets replaced with whatever enterprise credential mechanism the chosen LLM service uses
