On the narrative-layer model itself: this build uses a personal Gemini API key, a stand-in chosen because Generative AI Hub wasn't reachable on the trial tier. For a real deployment, that's not locked to Gemini specifically. Generative AI Hub is the natural first choice, mainly because it sits right alongside AI Core and RPT on the same governance and observability model this whole architecture already leans on. But the actual choice should follow whatever LLM the client already has enterprise access to and existing governance around, not force a specific vendor just because it's SAP's own.

What real security and performance hardening actually means here, not just a stated intent:

  • Secrets management through a proper credential store (e.g. SAP's Credential Store service) instead of environment variables set by hand.
  • Structured logging and observability, so a failed prediction or a slow call is something monitoring catches, not something a person discovers by accident.
  • Replacing the current broad except Exception handler with proper error boundaries that don't leak stack traces or internal details to the caller.
  • Rate limiting and input validation on the API itself, since right now it trusts whatever project ID it's handed.
  • Load testing and horizontal scaling for the backend, since this has only ever been tested against one request at a time.
  • A real CI/CD pipeline, including security scanning, instead of a manual cf push.

The enterprise architecture this POC doesn't attempt
Everything above is a POC-to-production checklist for the pieces this build actually touched. A real enterprise deployment involves decisions this series never had to make:

  • Data layer at scale. Datasphere stays the governance layer, but a production version needs a real data retention and archival policy for historical comparable projects, and the SQL view's performance needs revisiting once the comparable pool is thousands of projects deep, not hundreds.
  • Infrastructure and hyperscaler choice. This build runs on Cloud Foundry; a production version might instead run on Kyma (BTP's Kubernetes runtime) for better scaling and container-native deployment.
  • Governance beyond data. Model version tracking (which RPT/LLM version produced which historical prediction), audit logging of who saw which forecast and when, and a defined change-management process for updating the rescale or escalation logic, since that logic directly affects what gets written into a real plan.
  • Cost and lifecycle management. Monitoring AI Core and LLM usage costs at real volume, a defined SLA, and a documented process for retiring or replacing model versions over time.

What these four concepts could add later, even though none were needed here
Worth being specific about why Knowledge Graph, Company Memory, MCP, and A2A weren't needed, and what each would actually unlock if this use case grew beyond a POC:

  • Knowledge Graph. Today, "similar project" means matching on a flat set of attributes. A knowledge graph could model real relationships a flat table can't: projects sharing the same sponsor, the same resource pool, the same partner organisation, or sitting in the same program hierarchy. Comparable-project selection could then traverse those relationships instead of just filtering columns, catching similarity that attribute-matching alone misses.
  • Company Memory. Right now, nothing about a planner accepting, rejecting, or overriding a recommendation gets remembered anywhere. A persistent memory layer could track that over time, learning organisation-specific patterns the model itself has no access to: a particular manager who consistently overrides one milestone, a department whose projects reliably run over their initial forecast. That's institutional knowledge no amount of comparable-project matching alone can recover.
  • MCP. This build exposes its pipeline through purpose-built integrations, a Joule Action, a widget calling a REST endpoint, a scheduled script. Standardising that pipeline as MCP-compliant tools would mean any MCP-aware agent, not just the three consumers built here, could discover and call it without custom integration work each time, and it could compose more easily with other tools in a broader agent ecosystem.
  • A2A. Today, this forecast is a single-purpose tool a human consults. In an agent-to-agent architecture, this forecasting capability could become one input among several: coordinating with a budget-approval agent, a resource-planning agent, or a risk-assessment agent, autonomously, as part of a larger workflow rather than a standalone lookup a person triggers by hand.

None of this was necessary for what this POC set out to prove. But it's a genuine sketch of where the same underlying pipeline could grow, not a checklist of things that were simply missed.

Where This Actually Leaves Off

This POC started as a hands-on learning project, built against a real use case, not a promise that it would ship. It may or may not turn into a productive solution. What it does demonstrate is something narrower and more useful: how newer AI capabilities, layered onto existing systems, can take over the repetitive, manual parts of a job while still leaving the person in control at will, the way a driver stays behind the wheel with Tesla's FSD engaged, not replaced by it.

Feedback, pushback, and corrections are always welcome.

entry.title: Grounding Joule Agent on Your Own Documents Without Object Store
entry.content:
A hands-on walkthrough: bring your own AWS S3 bucket, ground it through SAP AI Core's Grounding Management, and expose it to a custom Joule agent with an SAP Build Action.
The full flow at a glance — from your S3 bucket to a grounded Joule agent.

 

 

 

If you follow the standard recipe for document grounding in Joule, you quickly run into two hard dependencies: the SAP Build Control Tower wizard and the BTP Object Store service. In plenty of real landscapes, neither is available — the Object Store instances are locked to stale S3 credentials you can't edit, and the Control Tower path isn't provisioned in your subaccount.

Here's the good news: neither is actually required. The grounding pipeline only needs S3-compatible credentials plus the SAP AI Core Document Grounding APIs. This post walks the complete, working path end to end, using screenshots from a live build.

What you'll stand up

  • A grounding pipeline over documents in your own AWS S3 bucket
  • Created through AI Launchpad's Grounding Management — no Control Tower, no scripting
  • Retrieval exposed to a Joule agent through a BTP destination + SAP Build Action

Before you start, you'll need

  • SAP AI Core on the extended plan (grounding capabilities require it)
  • A resource group carrying the ext.ai.sap.com/document-grounding label
  • An AWS account where you can create an S3 bucket and an IAM access key

Step 1 — Confirm your SAP AI Core instance (extended plan)

In BTP Cockpit → Services → Instances and Subscriptions, find your SAP AI Core instance. Grounding lives in the Generative AI Hub, which is only available on the extended plan — the standard plan won't do.


 SAP AI Core instances in BTP Cockpit

Open the instance and check the details: Service is SAP AI Core, Plan reads extended, and the status is Created. This instance's service key is what you'll upload in the next step.

 SAP AI Core instance details showing the extended plan

Step 2 — Register the AI API connection in AI Launchpad

AI Launchpad needs a connection to your AI Core tenant before it can manage grounding. Open Workspaces, then click Add in the top-right of AI API Connections.

 AI API Connections in AI Launchpad, with the Add button

Give the connection a name and upload the AI Core service key (default_aicore-key.json). The AI API URL, XSUAA URL, Client ID, and Client Secret populate automatically — leave the token suffix as /oauth/token. Click Create.

 Create AI API Connection dialog with auto-populated fields

Step 3 — Put your documents in an S3 bucket

This is the piece that replaces the BTP Object Store service. In your own AWS account, create an S3 bucket and upload the source documents you want the agent to ground on — here, a customer-support closed-cases PDF. (You can nest files in folders if you want to scope ingestion later.)

 S3 bucket objects: the source documents to ground on

You'll also need an IAM access key with read access to this bucket — keep the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key handy for the next step.

Step 4 — Store the S3 credentials as a Generic Secret

Now hand those credentials to AI Core. Go to SAP AI Core Administration → Generic Secrets → Add. Scope it to your grounding Resource Group, name it (e.g. cx-ai-object-store), set Document Repository Type to Amazon S3, and switch Document Grounding on.

 Add Generic Secret dialog for an Amazon S3 repository

Fill the key/value grid from your IAM key: URL, Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, Bucket, Host, and Region. One field trips everyone up — Authentication must be exactly NoAuthentication (that refers to proxy auth; your real S3 auth is the access key). Save.

Step 5 — Create the Data Repository (your grounding pipeline)

Here's where you skip both Control Tower and the Pipeline API. Open Generative AI Hub → Grounding Management → Create. Pick an Embedding Model (Text Embedding 3 Large), set Document Store Type to S3, and choose the Document Grounding Generic Secret you just created. Click Create.

Create Data Repository dialog in Grounding Management

That single action provisions the pipeline. It appears under Data Repositories with Source: S3 and an auto-generated pipeline-…-collection name.

 

The new S3 data repository in Grounding Management

Step 6 — Watch the ingestion and vectorization

Open the repository to see it work. AI Core fetches each document, splits it into chunks, generates embeddings, and stores them in the SAP HANA vector engine. The header shows Status: In Progress; the document shows Added with its chunk count (here, 757 chunks from one PDF).

 Data Repository Details showing ingestion in progress with 757 chunks

Wait for the status to reach Completed before you query. If it lands on Completed with errors, open the document list to see which files failed — usually scanned/image-only PDFs, empty objects, or unsupported types.

Step 7 — Create a BTP destination to AI Core

Your agent shouldn't juggle OAuth tokens — a destination handles that. In BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations, create an HTTP destination pointing at the AI Core API root, Proxy Type Internet, Authentication OAuth2ClientCredentials (Client ID / Secret and Token Service URL from the AI Core service key).

 BTP destination to AI Core with OAuth2ClientCredentials

The magic is in Additional Properties: set sap-joule-studio-document-grounding-ai-core = true and HTML5.DynamicDestination = true. The first makes the destination usable for grounding in the SAP Build / Joule tooling. Click Check Connection to confirm it's green.

 

Destination additional properties enabling grounding

Step 8 — Wrap retrieval as an SAP Build Action

This Action becomes the agent's "documents" tool. In SAP Build, add an Action that does a POST to /v2/lm/document-grounding/retrieval/search through the destination above. Define two header parameters — Content-Type: application/json and AI-Resource-Group: cx-ai-agent-grounding — and a body with query (string) and filters (array). That header is essential: it's how the call knows which resource group holds your pipeline.

 SAP Build Action calling the retrieval/search endpoint

A quick Test on this Action should return your top matching chunks — proof the RAG backend is live.

Step 9 — Add the Action to your Joule agent, then release

Finally, in Joule Studio, create your agent, set its instructions and model, and add the SAP Build Action as its retrieval tool — the drop-in replacement for the Control Tower documents tool. Ask a question that should hit your grounded content, confirm the answer cites your documents, and publish.

How it answers at runtime

CSR question → Joule agent → Documents tool (Build Action) → Retrieval API → HANA vector engine → top chunks → LLM grounded answer → CSR

Gotchas worth knowing

  • NoAuthentication, exactly. In the generic secret, values like "OAuth" or "S3" are rejected — the Authentication field wants NoAuthentication.
  • Carry the resource group as a header. If AI-Resource-Group isn't sent, the call runs against default, finds no pipeline, and 500s. Set it on the Action (as shown) or as URL.headers.AI-Resource-Group on the destination.
  • Point the destination at the right tenant. If the destination's OAuth credentials come from a different AI Core instance than your pipeline, retrieval returns an internal server error even with the header set.
  • Prefer a specific repository ID over ["*"]. The wildcard tries to resolve every repository in the group; if one is empty or broken, the whole search fails.
  • "Completed with errors" ≠ empty. The successfully-indexed docs are already searchable — fix or remove the failed files and re-sync.

Why this path is worth it

You trade the click-through convenience of the Control Tower wizard for owning the pipeline and retrieval wiring yourself. In return, you drop the dependency on the BTP Object Store service entirely and can ground on any S3-compatible bucket you control. For teams blocked by locked Object Store instances or an un-provisioned Control Tower, that trade is usually an easy yes.

API paths and field names are version-sensitive — verify them against the Document Grounding API on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub for your tenant.

entry.title: Agentic AI on BTP: Your Own Joule for Consultants, Connected to Your Own System
entry.content:
Introduction

What if you had something like Joule for Consultants, but connected to your own SAP system? Not just an assistant that knows the SAP documentation, but one that can also open the classes, CDS views and transports in the system you’re actually working on.

In my previous blog post, I introduced the dynamic multi-agent app: an orchestrator with specialist agents that are created, edited and reloaded at runtime, no redeploy needed: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-dynamic-multi-agent-on-demand-with-pydantic-ai/ba-p/14388032

That post ended with the claim that any MCP server can become a specialist agent with a row in a database. In this blog post, I’ll show you exactly how far that claim goes by configuring an ABAP agent that combines the SAP documentation MCP servers from @Marian_Zeis with ARC-1, an ADT MCP server that connects to a real ABAP system. The result behaves like a Joule for Consultants that knows your own landscape, purely by configuration.

Problem

Joule for Consultants is a nice idea: an AI assistant for SAP consultants with access to SAP knowledge, so you don’t have to dig through the Help Portal for every question. However, in practice it has two limitations that bother me.

First, it is not integrated into your own system. It can tell you how a CDS view works in general, but it has no idea which CDS views exist in your development system, how your Z-classes are built or what’s sitting in your open transport requests. As a consultant, that’s exactly the context you need, generic answers you can get from any chatbot.

Second, it comes with a cost per user. You pay per seat whether that consultant asks three questions a month or three hundred. For a small team that wants to experiment, that model is hard to justify.

Next to that, there is a bigger problem than Joule itself. Many companies simply don’t have a clear AI strategy yet, or they have Microsoft Copilot or something similar rolled out with not enough licenses to go around. And even when you do have such a license, it usually doesn’t allow you to connect your own MCP servers to it. So the SAP team ends up waiting for a company-wide decision that may take years.

This setup lets you get started on your own, within your SAP team, without waiting for that strategy. The only thing you need is BTP credits.

So what I actually want is:

  • Answers grounded in the official SAP documentation (ABAP keyword docs, SAP Help, RAP, CDS) instead of whatever the model remembers from training
  • Live access to my own ABAP system: search objects, read source code, run where-used analysis, check transports
  • The user’s own identity propagated to that system, so authorizations and audit still work
  • Pay for what you use (LLM tokens) instead of per user

Solution

The dynamic multi-agent app from the previous post already has everything needed for this, I just had to configure it. I created one new specialist agent, the ABAP Development Agent, and pointed it at three MCP servers:

  • The SAP Docs MCP server from Marian Zeis: SAP Help Portal, Discovery Center, released-object metadata and SAP Community content
  • ARC-1, also from Marian Zeis: a secure MCP proxy around the ADT REST API that connects to a real ABAP system

No custom code required. Just configuration. 🙂

The first server is publicly hosted, you can use them straight away without any setup. ARC-1 you deploy yourself, in my case as a Cloud Foundry app on BTP in front of my ABAP system.

To be clear, this doesn’t magically turn it into Joule. It won’t have SAP’s curated implementation content or learning journeys. Nevertheless, for the day-to-day questions a consultant or developer asks (“how does this statement work”, “where is this CDS view used”, “what’s in this class”), the combination of official docs plus your real system gets you surprisingly far.

What changed in the app: multiple MCP servers per agent

Since the previous post, the app supports connecting one agent to more than one MCP server. Each server is registered with its own auth mode:

Auth mode

When to use

How the user authenticates

jwt

BTP-hosted servers that trust this app’s XSUAA (HTTPS on *.hana.ondemand.com)

The user’s XSUAA JWT is forwarded on every request

oauth2

Servers with their own authorization server, like an ABAP system behind ARC-1

Per-user OAuth2 authorization_code, sign in once

none

Public servers that need no authentication

No token is sent

Next to that, there are a few more auth modes for the built-in toolsets: app-only client credentials, a BTP destination and a browser session you refresh by hand. For this scenario you only need the three above.

Registering an MCP server for an agent feels a lot like creating a destination in the BTP cockpit: you point at a URL, pick an auth type and you’re done.

The oauth2 mode is the interesting one for the ABAP scenario. The app supports Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591): tick “Dynamic registration”, fill in nothing else and on first use the app reads the MCP server’s OAuth metadata and registers itself as a client. The first time a user triggers the ABAP agent, the chat returns an Authorize link, the user signs in to the ABAP system once and from then on their own tokens are stored per user and forwarded on every call. This means the ABAP system sees the actual consultant, not a shared service account, per-user authorizations and audit are preserved.

In the meantime the app also got skills, workflows, scheduled job runs and a few built-in toolsets. You don’t need any of them for this scenario, so I’ll keep those for another post.

Configuring the ABAP agent

Everything happens in the admin UI. Since the previous post it got a SAPUI5 version, served at /ui5admin next to the original one at /admin. Both use the same backend and the same database, so it doesn’t matter which one you take, only the labels are a bit different. The screenshots below are from the UI5 admin.

  • Open /ui5admin and click “New agent” in the Agents list:

  • In the General panel, fill in the name, description and instructions for the specialist. The “Enabled” and “Available in chat” switches are on by default.
  • Next, add the servers in the Toolsets panel with the “Add toolset” button. For each one you fill in the URL and pick the auth mode, for ARC-1 you also tick “Dynamic registration”:

 

 

One thing to keep in mind here: by default only HTTPS URLs on *.hana.ondemand.com can be registered for the authenticated modes. Public servers on auth mode none are not restricted, so the two documentation servers work straight away. If your ARC-1 runs somewhere else, you need to put its URL in the MCP_URL_ALLOWLIST env var of the app.

  • Once saved, go to Settings and click “Reload” in the Lifecycle panel. This rebuilds the orchestrator in memory, the new specialist is available in the chat from the very next message. You can validate if this was successful by asking a question in the chat and checking that the steps of the new specialist show up in the answer.

Because agent definitions are just data, the whole thing can also be captured as a JSON snapshot with the Export and Import buttons in Settings. An export carries the orchestrator instructions, the skills, the agents and the workflows. Below is the agent part of it, which is also included as agents.seed.json in the repo:

{
  "version": 1,
  "orchestrator_instructions": "You are an orchestration agent for SAP development and operations tasks. You do not perform technical work directly, instead you interpret the user's intent and delegate to the appropriate specialist agent, then synthesize their output into a clear response. ...",
  "agents": [
    {
      "name": "ABAP Development Agent",
      "description": "Search and retrieve SAP product documentation: ABAP, SAPUI5, Fiori, CAP, BTP services, and general SAP developer docs. Use for reference lookups and how-to questions.",
      "instructions": "An autonomous ABAP development assistant that combines authoritative SAP documentation lookup with live system access via ARC-1. ...",
      "mcp_servers": [
        {
          "url": "http://mcp-sap-docs.marianzeis.de/mcp",
          "auth_mode": "none"
        },
        {
          "url": "https://<your-arc-1-deployment>/mcp",
          "auth_mode": "oauth2",
          "oauth": {
            "dcr": true,
            "has_client_secret": false
          }
        }
      ],
      "enabled": true
    }
  ]
}

The full instructions are in the repo, the short version: the agent is told it can ground answers in the ABAP/RAP documentation, read and navigate objects in the connected system via ADT, compute CDS blast-radius, run linting, diagnose dumps, query system tables and manage transports.

You could argue that one agent with three MCP servers gets a rather long tool list for a single specialist. So far it works fine, the servers expose focused tools (ARC-1 deliberately ships 12 intent-based tools instead of 200+ endpoint wrappers). Splitting documentation and system access into two specialists is always possible later, it’s just another row in the database.

The result

Once the agent is reloaded, the chat behaves like a consultant assistant. Asking “can you explain me how to create a cds view in an abap system?” makes the orchestrator delegate to the specialist, which grounds its answer in the ABAP documentation:

Next to that, questions like “show me the source of class ZCL_…” or “where is CDS view Z… used?” go through ARC-1 into the connected system, after the one-time Authorize step, with the user’s own credentials.

 

A word on safety: ARC-1 is read-only by default. Writes, data preview and free SQL each require explicit flags on the server and package allowlists restrict where anything can be created. For a consultant assistant, read-only is exactly what you want to start with.

Cost

There is no per-user license anywhere in this setup. The moving parts are the python app and its approuter on Cloud Foundry, a PostgreSQL instance, the HTML5 application repository for the UI5 admin, the ARC-1 deployment and the LLM consumption through SAP AI Core’s Generative AI Hub. You pay for tokens when people actually use it. Ten consultants who ask ten questions a day cost you their token usage, not ten seats.

Everything runs on BTP, so all of it is covered by your existing BTP contract. If you’re on a consumption-based model with credits left at the end of the contract year, this is a nice way to turn them into something your team actually benefits from instead of losing them.

Conclusion

The previous post promised that any MCP server can become a specialist agent with a row in a database. This post cashed in on that promise: by registering three existing MCP servers in the admin UI, the platform turned into an SAP assistant that knows both the official documentation and my own ABAP system, with the user’s identity flowing through on every call. In the end, the “own Joule for Consultants” was a configuration exercise, not a development project.

Contributions and feedback are welcome! The full source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app

entry.title: Passed SAP Generative AI Developer (C_AIG_2604) with 100% — AI Was Fast, Verification Made It Right
entry.content:
Introduction

A few days ago, I sat for the SAP Certified – SAP Generative AI Developer (C_AIG_2604) certification, SAP's hands-on System-Based Assessment built around the Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Launchpad. I walked away with a 100% score.


That's a nice number to share, it's not really why I'm writing this.

There are already a couple of great posts on SAP Community covering the exam's submission mechanics in real detail — naming conventions, the orchestration-scenario save gotcha, manually adding System/User/Assistant blocks. If you haven't read those yet, go do that first; I won't repeat all of it here. What I haven't seen anyone write about yet is something I think matters more than any UI quirk: how easy it is to let AI assistance quietly cost you the exam, even while it's helping you pass it.

The Format Is Genuinely Different

This isn't a traditional multiple-choice SAP certification. It's a timed, hands-on lab where you build real deliverables — prompt templates, in this case — directly inside SAP AI Launchpad. It's also explicitly open-book, AI assistance included: SAP lets you use official documentation and even SAP Joule for Consultants while the clock is running. That's the whole point of this post, actually, because that openness is exactly where things get interesting.

The Real Trap With AI-Assisted Exams

Here's the thing nobody tells you going in: being allowed to use AI doesn't mean using it is automatically safe for your score.

AI Is Open-Book Here — That's a Double-Edged Sword

When AI hands you a confident, complete-looking solution, it's tempting to just copy, paste, and move to the next task. A 3-hour exam can start to feel like it's over in under one. That speed is deceptive — grading in this exam comes down to precise, unglamorous details: exact naming conventions, correct scenario assignments, exact version numbers. None of that is something AI can verify for you, because it's inside a live system it's never actually seen render. Copy-pasting confidently without cross-checking against the instructions is how small misses quietly pile up — and you won't find out until the result lands, by which point it's too late to fix.

And this isn't just theory — a couple of colleagues told me afterward that they'd needed more than one attempt, missing the 76% cut score by a narrow margin each time. When they went back to figure out why, it wasn't the prompt engineering that let them down at all. It came down to exactly this: a naming convention slightly off here, an instruction followed a little loosely there.

What actually got me to 100% wasn't AI doing the work faster. It was using the full time available, treating AI strictly as a drafting partner rather than an autopilot, and manually re-verifying every single save — template name, scenario, version — against the instructions before moving forward. Slow and deliberate, even with AI doing the heavy lifting, beat fast and confident every time. If you take one thing from this post, take that: the exam isn't really testing whether you can use AI. It's testing whether you'll still check its work.

SAP Joule for Consultants (J4C) — Nice to Have, Not a Crutch

During the exam you get two separate windows — your live AI Launchpad exam system, and SAP Joule for Consultants (J4C). Both open from the systems menu before you start, free, available the whole time.

Honestly, I barely touched it. I stayed heads-down in my exam tab, telling myself I'd try it if I got stuck — but as I neared the finish line, I chose to lock in Confirm Completion early rather than gamble the last few minutes on a tool I hadn't used yet.

My honest take, looking back: J4C is genuinely useful for exploring unfamiliar concepts on the fly. But if you've actually worked through the Learning Journey beforehand, you likely won't need it much — you'll already know the terms and workflows cold. SAP seems to have built it into the exam less as a safety net and more to give you a taste of how you'd lean on J4C in a real client scenario when you're stuck. Good to know it's there. Better if you don't have to reach for it.

A Few Lessons Worth Adding to What's Already Out There

Beyond the discipline point above, a handful of things stood out as genuinely useful, on top of what the existing tips posts already cover:

Validate Your JSON Before You Trust It

"Please respond in JSON" and actually clean, parseable JSON are two different things. A stray markdown fence, an extra space or line break outside the structure, a smart quote instead of a straight one — none of that is visible just by eyeballing the text, especially when you're skimming a long response quickly. I got into the habit of pasting outputs into a quick external JSON validator before relying on them for the next step — a search for "JSON validator" turns up several free, reliable ones. Cheap insurance, and it catches exactly the kind of invisible formatting slip that's easy to miss on screen but breaks things downstream.

Treat Prompt Templates Like Living, Versioned Artifacts

Rather than rewriting prompts from scratch at each stage, build incrementally — a solid base (clear system role, defined output schema), then layered, deliberate versions for each refinement. This mirrors how you'd manage prompts in a real production setup through the Prompt Registry, so it's worth the habit regardless of the exam. Versions are cumulative too: whatever you saved last time carries forward, so you can safely open the latest version as your starting point rather than hunting back through earlier ones — just delete any old Assistant-role entry first, or a stale answer can quietly ride along into the new version without you noticing.

Before you submit, open Prompt Management → Templates and pull up the full list of every prompt template and version you've saved. Cross-check it against the task instructions, version by version. Two minutes, and it's the easiest way to catch a skipped or mislabeled version before it costs you.

A "Prompt" Isn't a "Prompt Template"

Small distinction, easy to trip over when you're moving fast: clicking Run in the Prompt Editor and actually clicking Save Template are two different actions. It sounds obvious written down, but more than once I caught myself about to move to the next task after just running a prompt — the fix is just a habit: always confirm you've hit Save Template, not only Run, before you consider a version done.

Prompt Hardening Isn't Optional Once It Touches a Real Workflow

Explicit negative instructions — what the model should refuse to do, how it handles attempts to hijack its role, firm boundaries on what data it can expose — belong in early versions, not as an afterthought.

Model Evaluation Is a Real Skill, Not a Checkbox

Comparing outputs across different models taught me "correct" isn't binary. The real differences show up in how actionable and complete the details are, not just whether classification labels technically match.

Submit With Real Margin

Simple, but worth repeating: don't wait until the last minute. Hands-on labs occasionally have UI hiccups, and buffer time is what turns a hiccup into a non-event instead of a disaster.

If Something Looks Broken, It Probably Isn't

Twice during the exam I hit a Run button that just wouldn't respond. Both times the fix was the same: click into the System role field, the User role field, and the variable's Current Value field, one at a time, then try again — or switch to a different model in the Model Configuration panel if that still doesn't budge. It's rarely the system actually failing; it's usually just the editor waiting for you to register a change somewhere. Worth knowing before you start second-guessing your setup or burning time troubleshooting something that isn't really broken.

One more small habit that saves grief later: before you save anything, check the top-right corner of SAP AI Launchpad and confirm your exact candidate ID (shown in the format CERT####). It sounds unnecessary until you're deep into template version four and realize you never actually checked it matches what you assumed.

A Few Environment Quirks Worth Knowing Before You Start

None of these are exam content — just orientation. But not knowing them cost me a few confused minutes I didn't need to lose, so here's what I wish I'd known walking in:

  • The Templates list isn't just yours. Depending on how the resource group is set up, you may see other candidates' saved templates sitting right alongside your own in Prompt Management → Templates. It's disorienting the first time — just search for your own template name specifically rather than scrolling, and you'll find your work without second-guessing whether something got mixed up.

     

  • Generative AI Hub → Orchestration will look empty, and that's fine. I went looking for a configuration to set up there before realizing the exam doesn't actually need one — your deliverables live entirely in your saved prompt templates, not in an Orchestration config.
     
  • The Prompt Management → Prompts tab staying at zero is expected too. That's for one-off, ad-hoc runs — not where your actual saved work shows up. Don't go looking for your templates there.
     
  • Opening a specific version only shows you that version. If you want to see the full list of everything you've saved so far, go back to Prompt Management → Templates rather than expecting to page through versions from within a single one.

None of this is difficult once you know it. It's just the kind of thing that's obvious in hindsight and mildly maddening in the moment — so hopefully this saves you the minute or two I spent frowning at my screen.

Where to Prepare

1. The Official Learning Journey

If you want a structured starting point, SAP's own Solving Business Problems using SAP's Generative AI Hub learning journey covers the ground well, especially its hands-on practice course with live system access. It's already been pointed to elsewhere on Community, and for good reason — it's genuinely the right place to build real muscle memory in AI Launchpad before exam day.

2. Live "Get Certified" Sessions

SAP also runs a free, live-led "Get Certified" session series specifically for this exam — a kick-off session plus two content review sessions and a wrap-up, walking through exam mechanics and key topics with an actual SAP instructor. Worth checking the schedule (requires SAP Learning Hub login): Get Certified: SAP Certified - SAP Generative AI Developer.


Further Reading

Communities like this one work because people share what they've learned and point others toward good work, not just their own. Full credit to the folks below, whose posts I actually leaned on while preparing for and passing this exam — their tips and experiences genuinely helped:

  • C_AIG SAP Generative AI Developer Exam — Tips for the System-Based Assessment by neilaspin — the deepest dive I've seen into the submission mechanics specifically: naming conventions, the orchestration-scenario save gotcha, and manually building out System/User/Assistant message blocks.
  • SAP Certified – SAP Generative AI Developer | Preparation Guide & How to Ace It (C_AIG_2604) by DheerajHJ — a solid task-by-task strategy walkthrough, including the useful framing of the exam as "Exercise 5" of the Learning Journey.
  • My Experience with SAP Generative AI Developer Exam (C_AIG): Excellent Hands-On Format, One Setback by hitenbhanushali — a candid account of the open-book format done well, plus a cautionary note about the Confirm Completion button not always behaving in the final minutes. Worth reading for that alone.


Final Thoughts

This certification felt less like a memory test and more like a genuine day-in-the-life exercise for anyone building generative AI solutions on SAP BTP. But the most important skill it tests isn't prompt design — it's judgment. AI will hand you a fast, confident answer. Whether you slow down and verify it anyway is what actually separates a pass from a fail.

Good luck. If you're prepping for this one, drop your questions in the comments — happy to help where I can.

entry.title: From AI-Ready Data to Agent-Ready Data
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series :

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

For years, many data architecture conversations started with the same question: How do we bring data together so the business can report on it?

With AI agents, I think we need to add another question:

What does an agent need to understand before we allow it to recommend — or take — an action?

A dashboard may tell us that overdue receivables have increased. An agent could go much further. It might be asked to identify the customers behind the increase, check disputed invoices, recommend the next step, and even create a follow-up task.

That is a very different demand on the data foundation. Every one of those steps requires more than a clean table.

What changes for the data foundation?

An agent needs to understand the agreed meaning of a measure such as DSO. It needs to know the relationships between customers, invoices, and disputes. It needs to understand where each figure came from, how fresh it is, and which permissions apply to both the user and the agent.

Just as importantly, there needs to be a clear boundary between explaining a situation and changing it.

An AI response can sound completely convincing even when one of these foundations is missing.

Gartner describes the move toward agent-ready data in terms of whether data is suitable for agentic use and whether the agent is using it in a valid way. McKinsey also emphasizes semantics, reusable data products, relationships, governance, and observability.

I find both perspectives useful because they move the discussion away from a broad statement such as “our data is clean” and toward something much more specific:

Is this data ready for this agent, this user, this decision, and this action?

How I would approach this in an SAP landscape

SAP Business Data Cloud and its data products can provide a governed starting point.

SAP Datasphere can help model business meaning and make data easier to discover and consume.

SAP Knowledge Graph also appears in SAP’s longer-term architecture vision as a semantic grounding layer for agents. I would treat that as architectural direction rather than assuming that every capability is already available in every customer landscape today.

If I were starting a customer workshop, I would begin with five questions:

  1. What decision should the agent support?
  2. Which facts would an experienced employee check before making that decision?
  3. Who owns the definitions and quality checks behind those facts?
  4. What is the agent allowed to see and do?
  5. How will we trace its answer back to the supporting evidence?

The answers to those questions tell us what data products, semantics, documents, and controls are actually required.

For a first release, I would often start with an agent that explains a situation and cites the supporting records.

If users can validate the answer consistently, we can then assess whether a controlled action makes sense.

This is where I see the role of the data architect evolving. Our job is no longer only to deliver the right number. We also need to establish its meaning, reliability, context, and permitted use inside a business process.

A practical way to make this real is to start small: one question, one user role, and one proposed action.

That makes the architecture testable.

If the answer changes when the role or proposed action changes, the underlying data product may still be valuable, but the agent design probably needs a more precise boundary.

This also gives the architect an important role in adoption conversations.

We can bring finance, process, security, and data teams around one concrete scenario and make their assumptions visible. If they disagree, that disagreement is useful evidence. It tells us where the design is still unclear.

It is much cheaper to resolve those questions in a workshop than after an automated action has already been taken.

entry.title: Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent?
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

A customer may have a governed purchase order data product and ask whether it can be used to build an agent. My answer would be to look first at what the agent is expected to do. Imagine an agent helping a procurement team with delayed orders. A user asks why an order is late and what should happen next.

 

Figure: The five readiness checks for a purchase order data product.

Five checks before the agent uses it

First, define the business meaning. Does late refer to the original delivery date or the latest confirmed date? Is a partially delivered item late? Which status is authoritative? These questions sound basic until an agent has to explain an exception without a buyer beside it.

Second, map the context. The answer may depend on the supplier, contract, goods receipt and current delivery commitment. If that commitment is in an inaccessible email, the agent should say its information is incomplete.

Third, check trust. When were the records updated? Are the fields complete? Can we trace the figures to their source? An unposted goods receipt can make the order look late even when the goods have arrived.

Fourth, test access end to end. A buyer may see only orders within a purchasing organization. The agent’s data access and every tool call must respect the relevant scope. SAP Datasphere data access controls can help restrict rows in protected objects, but the complete path still needs to be tested.

Fifth, define the action. Explaining a delay, recommending a supplier call, creating a task and changing a purchase order have different consequences. The right to read an order is not the right to change it.

A useful starting outcome

I would start with an agent that explains the exception, shows its evidence and points out missing information. Procurement users can then assess whether the result is dependable. Once that works, the business can define which follow-up actions are appropriate and where approval belongs.

The architecture question is not simply whether a data product exists. It is whether the data product and its surrounding context are fit for the exact decision and level of autonomy we expect.

For the purchase order pilot, I would ask the buyer to walk through two real exceptions. One should have complete records; the other should include a missing or conflicting commitment. Those cases show whether the agent can explain uncertainty rather than turn an incomplete picture into a confident instruction.

The same review should include the user experience. If an agent lacks the contract, it should tell the buyer what it checked and suggest who can confirm the commitment. That response is still useful. It respects the limit of the available information and helps the person complete the work.

entry.title: What an AI infra engineer sees when opening SAP's AI stack (1/3): the model gateway
entry.content:
I recently passed the SAP Generative AI Developer certification, which gave me a first tour of SAP AI Core, the Generative AI Hub, and the pieces around them. I'm new to the SAP world, so I'm going to write down what I learn as I go. This is the first of three posts.

The series follows the stack from the bottom of a model call outward.

  • Part 1 covers the gateway layer: orchestration, modules, fallback, billing, and SDKs.
  • Part 2 will look at serving your own models and retrieval on HANA.
  • Part 3 will move up to agents, A2A and MCP, and what I take from the stack as a whole.

A word on what this is. It's a map, not a benchmark. I read documentation, SDK repositories, reference architectures, and community posts, and I'm sharing what stood out to someone who spends his days on the non-SAP version of this problem. Everything here reflects late September 2026. SAP's docs move, so check the dates on anything you plan to build on.

Here's the shape of it before I get into any of the pieces individually:


The familiar part: a model gateway

The Generative AI Hub is a capability of SAP AI Core and SAP AI Launchpad. SAP's own docs say it extends AI Core rather than replacing it. AI Core is the runtime, and the hub sits on top.

The piece I'd call the gateway is the orchestration service. You create an orchestration deployment inside a resource group (the default resource group already has one), authenticate with the service key from your AI Core instance, and send requests to it.

The API is harmonized, which means SAP took the OpenAI API as the standard and maps other providers onto it. Switching models is a change to a model name string. Anthropic models use a double-dash convention, for example anthropic--claude-4.5-sonnet. The SDK's model table currently lists models from Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, OpenAI, Cohere, and Perplexity. The authoritative list lives in SAP Note 3437766, which also carries token conversion rates, rate limits, and deprecation dates. I like having deprecation dates sitting next to the model list. Anyone who has had a model retired underneath a running product will know why.

The module pipeline

On top of plain model calls, a request can switch on modules: templating, grounding, translation, data masking, and content filtering. The docs also list tool calling, structured output, reasoning parameters, streaming, and embeddings on the same API.

The modules run as a pipeline in one call, and each module's output feeds the next. SAP's docs say the order is defined centrally. You configure the modules and leave out the optional ones, but you don't reorder them. I didn't see a way to insert a step of my own. If you're used to gateway middleware you write yourself, that's a real difference. For guardrails, it's probably what you want anyway.

The fixed order looks like this:

  • Templating: Fills in your prompt placeholders.
  • Masking: Masks PII (Personally Identifiable Information) before it leaves you, via SAP Data Privacy Integration.
  • Grounding: Pulls retrieved context from the HANA vector store.
  • Filtering: Runs a safety check on input and output, via Azure Content Safety or Llama Guard 3.
  • Model call: Sends the request to the LLM. On a timeout or error in a non-streaming call, it retries the next fallback config.

Optional modules are just left out of the chain, not moved around in it.

Two modules deserve a closer look:

  • Data masking: Uses SAP Data Privacy Integration. You can anonymize, which is irreversible, or pseudonymize, which lets the service put the original values back into the response.
  • Content filtering: Supports Azure Content Safety and Llama Guard 3 (the 8B model). Azure covers hate, violence, sexual content, and self-harm on a severity scale, and it has a prompt shield option.

Fallback, since that's an important part of my job

Routing and failover are what I know best, so I went looking. You give the client an ordered list of module configurations, and the service tries them in sequence until one succeeds. Each entry can carry its own model, parameters, system prompt, filtering, and masking settings. So your fallback model can run under different rules than your primary.

A few details from the SDK docs that I'd want to know before relying on this:

  • There is a timeout setting on the model. In non-streaming calls, exceeding it triggers the fallback. It applies to the individual LLM call, not the whole orchestration request.
  • For streaming, the fallback happens before the stream starts. The service will not switch models in the middle of a stream.
  • Content filter hits and invalid input errors do not trigger a fallback.

What I did not find in the docs I read is weighted routing, cost-based or latency-based routing, or circuit breaker state. That doesn't mean they don't exist, only that I didn't see them. The open-source and hosted gateways people run today, such as LiteLLM, llmrouter, and Portkey, document routing, caching, retries, and spend tracking, so if you need those knobs you may still want your own layer.

Billing and SDKs

Generative AI usage is metered in tokens and converted to capacity units against your BTP contract, but which costs apply depends on whether you're calling a hosted model or running your own:

 Foundation models (hosted by SAP)Custom / BYOM models (you serve them)
Billed by Tokens, converted to capacity unitsCompute, storage, and an hourly baseline
Compute, storage, baseline chargesWaivedCharged; baseline is capped 
CoversCalling GPT, Claude, Gemini, and so on through orchestration, plus grounding

Running Ollama, vLLM, or your own inference server on AI Core

The official SDKs cover JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, and Python, all Apache 2.0. The JavaScript one is the easiest to see the shape of, since it's split into separate npm packages:

PackageCovers
ai-apiScenario and workflow management: training pipelines, batch inference, deploying inference endpoints
orchestrationThe orchestration service itself: templating, grounding, masking, filtering, fallback, tool calling
foundation-modelsCalling a specific deployed model directly, without going through orchestration
document-groundingThe Pipeline, Vector, and Retrieval APIs for RAG
prompt-registryStoring and versioning prompts
langchainLangChain-compatible model clients, built on top of the foundation-model clients

Python and Java package it a bit differently, but cover the same ground. I write mostly Go, and I didn't find an official Go SDK.

There's a workaround that I found interesting. SAP contributed a provider to LiteLLM, reached with a sap/ prefix, covering chat completions and embeddings. That means you can put your own gateway in front of SAP's, and SAP's orchestration becomes one upstream among several.

So far, the SAP stack looks familiar in the places closest to the model call: one gateway API, a fixed module pipeline, ordered fallback, contract-based billing, and SDKs for the main supported languages. The more SAP-specific part starts when the platform stops being only a gateway.

In part 2, I'll look at AI Core as a runtime for your own models, the document grounding APIs, and HANA's vector engine.

entry.title: Using SAP Integration Suite AI Adapter to turn integration failures into actionable insights
entry.content:
Using SAP Integration Suite AI Adapter to turn integration failures into actionable insights

Introduction

Integration monitoring is an essential part of every integration landscape.

When customers have hundreds or even thousands of integrations running every day, monitoring becomes critical to identifying failed messages, understanding what happened, and taking corrective actions.

But there is an important question that goes beyond simply detecting a failure:

When an integration fails, how quickly can we understand what happened and what we should do next?

In many integration scenarios, the monitoring platform tells us that something went wrong. The next step still requires a person to open the Message Processing Log (MPL), analyze the failed step, inspect the backend response, and determine the probable root cause.

This is where I see an interesting opportunity for AI.

Instead of using AI to replace integration monitoring, we can use it to add an intelligence layer on top of the monitoring process.

In this blog, I will show a Proof of Concept using SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration, SAP Generative AI Hub, and the AI Adapter, where an integration failure automatically triggers an AI-based analysis that can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

The Challenge: An Integration Error Is Often Just the Beginning

Imagine that an integration fails and the monitoring team receives:

 

 
HTTP 400 - Bad Request
Technically, this is useful information. However, from an operational perspective, the investigation has just started.

The support analyst may need to:

  1. Open the Message Processing Log.
  2. Identify the failed step.
  3. Inspect the backend response.
  4. Understand which business process was being executed.
  5. Identify the probable root cause.
  6. Determine the business impact.
  7. Decide whether the message can be safely reprocessed.

    When this happens occasionally, this process is manageable.

    When it happens hundreds of times across a large integration landscape, the amount of manual analysis can become significant.

    This led me to explore a simple question:

    What if AI could perform the first level of incident analysis when an integration fails?

    The Concept

    The idea is not to replace the Message Processing Log or the existing integration monitoring capabilities.

    Instead, the architecture adds an AI-assisted analysis layer.

    The traditional approach looks like this:

     

     
    Integration Failure
        ↓
Monitoring
        ↓
Message Processing Log
        ↓
Manual Investigation
        ↓
Root Cause
        ↓
Action
    The proposed approach is:

     

     
    Integration Failure
        ↓
Exception Subprocess
        ↓
Collect Error Context
        ↓
AI Adapter
        ↓
AI Incident Analysis
        ↓
Operational Notification
        ↓
Human Investigation / Action
    The AI provides the initial interpretation, while the existing monitoring capabilities remain available for detailed technical investigation.

    Use Case

    The use case is based on a Sales Order integration between an external application and SAP S/4HANA.

    The external application sends a Sales Order request to SAP S/4HANA through SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration.

    Under normal conditions, the integration processes the request and the Sales Order is created successfully.

    However, if an error occurs during the integration, the scenario follows a different path. Instead of simply reporting the technical failure, the integration captures the available error context and sends it to the AI Adapter for analysis.

    One important architectural principle here is that the AI processing only happens when an error occurs.

    The normal business flow does not need to invoke the AI model.

    This is an important point when thinking about AI in integration scenarios:

    AI does not necessarily need to be part of every transaction. It can be activated when intelligence is actually needed.

    Technology Components

    The solution combines several capabilities of the SAP ecosystem:

     

     

     

     

    The key point is that these components are combined into an incident-analysis flow, rather than using AI as part of every normal transaction.

    Setting Up SAP Generative AI Hub

    To implement this scenario, the AI capabilities are provided through SAP Generative AI Hub.

    The Generative AI Hub provides a governed environment for accessing generative AI models and incorporating them into enterprise scenarios.

    For this example, the AI model is used to analyze integration incidents and generate a structured troubleshooting response.

     

     

    The exact model configuration can vary depending on the available models and the customer's SAP environment.

    For this scenario, the important concept is not the specific model itself, but the ability to expose generative AI capabilities to the integration flow in a controlled way.

    Configuring the AI Adapter

    Once the AI environment is available, the next step is to configure the AI Adapter in SAP Cloud Integration.

    The AI Adapter is used to invoke the AI capabilities from within the integration flow.

     

     

     

     

     

     

     In the Service Key, the endpoint is provided under serviceurls as AI_API_URL. This value is used as the API endpoint when configuring the connection to SAP AI Core.

    OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials

    To connect SAP AI Launchpad and SAP Integration Suite to SAP AI Core, the required authentication information is obtained from a Service Key of the SAP AI Core service instance.

    In SAP BTP Cockpit, navigate to the subaccount where SAP AI Core is provisioned and open the corresponding SAP AI Core service instance.

    From the service instance, create a new Service Key and download or copy its credentials. 

    In this scenario, the AI Adapter is placed inside the Exception Subprocess.

    This is intentional.

    The AI service is not invoked for every successful Sales Order.

    It is invoked when an integration failure occurs and additional analysis is required.

    This creates an architecture where AI becomes an on-demand intelligence layer for integration incidents.

    Defining the AI Prompt

    The next step is defining what the AI should do with the integration error.

    Rather than asking a generic question such as:

    "What is wrong with this integration?"

    the prompt defines a structured troubleshooting task.

    For example:

     

     
    You are an SAP Integration troubleshooting assistant.

Analyze the following integration incident.

SAP S/4HANA Error:
${property.error_message}

MPL ID:
${property.mpl_id}

Provide the analysis using the following structure:

1. Incident Summary
2. Probable Root Cause
3. Business Impact
4. Evidence
5. Investigation Points
6. Recommended Actions
7. Can the message be safely reprocessed?
8. Priority Level
    The structure of the prompt is important.

    The goal is not simply to generate a natural-language answer.

    The goal is to produce an output that can be used by an integration operations or support team.

    Step 1 — Capture the Error Context

    The first step in the Exception Subprocess is to capture the relevant error information generated by the integration.

    For example, the HTTP layer may provide:

     

     
    Bad Request : 400 : HTTP/1.1
     

    However, the backend response can contain much more meaningful information:

     

     
    Material TG1100 is not defined for sales org. 1410,
distr. chan. 10, OrProperty 'SoldToParty' has invalid value '14100009000'

     

    The integration can extract the relevant error information and make it available to the AI analysis.

    This distinction is important.

    A generic HTTP status tells us:

    Something failed.

    The backend error can help explain:

    Why it failed.

    This is one of the key requirements for an AI-assisted monitoring scenario:

    The AI needs meaningful context, not just an HTTP status code.

    Step 2 — AI Analysis with the AI Adapter

    Once the relevant error context has been prepared, the Exception Subprocess invokes the AI Adapter.

    The AI receives the error information together with the instructions defined in the prompt.

    The goal is to transform a technical exception into a structured incident analysis.

    For example:

     

     
    Technical Error
       ↓
AI Adapter
       ↓
Generative AI Model
       ↓
Structured Incident Analysis
    This is where the solution starts moving from monitoring toward intelligent operations.

    Step 3 — Processing the AI Response

    The AI Adapter returns the generated incident analysis.
    The response can then be passed to the notification step, where it is included in the operational notification sent to the support or integration team.

     

     

     
    The result is no longer just:

     

     
    HTTP 400
    Instead, the support team receives a structured analysis.

    For example:

     

     
    1. Incident Summary:
Sales Order creation failed in SAP S/4HANA.

2. Probable Root Cause:
Material TG1100 is not maintained for sales organization
1410 and distribution channel 10.

3. Business Impact:
The Sales Order could not be created.

4. Evidence:
Material = TG1100
Sales Organization = 1410
Distribution Channel = 10

5. Investigation Points:
Verify the material master and sales area data.

6. Recommended Actions:
Extend the material to the required sales area or
use a valid material.

7. Can the message be safely reprocessed?
No. The master data issue should be corrected first.

8. Priority Level:
High.
    The important difference is that the system has moved from:

    Error Detection

    to:

    Contextual Analysis

    Step 4 — Turning AI Analysis into an Operational Notification

    Once the AI has analyzed the integration error, the result can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

    For this Proof of Concept, the AI-generated analysis is included in an automated notification.

     

    The important point is that the notification is not intended to replace the monitoring platform.

    It provides an AI-generated first analysis before the analyst starts the deeper investigation.

    In our example, the notification is sent by email. However, the same AI-generated analysis could also be delivered through other channels, such as Microsoft Teams, SAP Alert Notification service, or an IT service management platform.

    Where Could This Go Next?

    This approach opens several possibilities for extending AI-assisted integration monitoring and intelligent operations.

    Automatic Error Classification

    Errors could be classified into categories such as:

    • Authentication
    • Authorization
    • Connectivity
    • Mapping
    • Transformation
    • Master Data
    • Business Validation
    • Backend Errors
      Final Result

      Final Result

      After the integration failure is detected and analyzed, the AI-generated incident analysis can be delivered to the team responsible for monitoring and support.

      In this example, the result is delivered by email. However, the same approach could be used to automatically create an incident or service ticket, send a notification through Microsoft Teams, or integrate with an IT service management platform.

      The important point is that the support team receives more than a technical error message. The AI provides a structured first analysis that can help the team understand the incident and decide what to investigate next.

      Example 1 — Invalid Material in SAP S/4HANA

       

      Example 2 — Invalid Business Partner in SAP S/4HANA

       

       

       

       

       

      Conclusion

      This could help operations teams prioritize and route incidents.

      When an integration fails, knowing that it failed is only the first step.

      The real challenge is understanding what happened, why it happened, and what should be investigated next.

      In this scenario, SAP Integration Suite, the AI Adapter, and SAP Generative AI Hub were combined to add an AI-assisted incident analysis layer to an existing integration monitoring process.

      The goal is not to replace monitoring, logs, or the expertise of integration teams. Instead, AI can help transform technical error information into a structured starting point for investigation and action.

      As integration landscapes continue to grow in complexity, this approach opens the door to a different way of thinking about integration operations:

      From detecting failures to understanding incidents.

      And perhaps the next step is not simply asking:

      "Did my integration fail?"

      but rather:

      "What happened, why did it happen, and what should I do next?"

       
      SAP Integration Suite
      Cloud Integration  
      SAP AI Core

entry.title: Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series :

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

 

When a customer says a data product is ready, I like to ask who will answer when an agent gives the wrong answer. The schema may be clear and the pipeline may run every day. But if a business definition changes or a source starts arriving late, somebody must own that change.

 

Figure: The owner remains accountable for changes and exceptions after a data product is published.

Treat the interface as a product

Take a supplier performance data product. Its consumers may include a dashboard, a sourcing analyst and an agent that recommends which supplier needs attention. Each consumer needs to know the unit of analysis, refresh schedule, permitted use, expected quality and contact for an issue. A table name and column list tell only part of that story.

I would define a small product agreement: business purpose, owner, source systems, grain, measure definitions, freshness target, quality rules, sensitivity and access method. I would also describe what happens when the schema or a business rule changes. These are design choices for the team that publishes and consumes the data, not properties I would assume exist automatically.

The agent changes the support model

A human analyst may notice a missing country or an unusual supplier name and investigate. An agent might continue to the next step before anyone notices. That makes ownership and change communication more urgent. If a quality rule fails, should the agent stop, answer with a warning or route the case to a person? The data product owner and process owner should decide together.

SAP Business Data Cloud provides a data product approach, and the catalog helps users find and inspect the assets available to them. My recommendation is to add a clear operating agreement around each high-value product used by agents. Start with one use case, test the agreement with its consumers, then reuse what works in the next domain.

The strongest sign of a mature data product is not that it has been published. It is that a consumer knows what it means, whether it can be trusted today and who will resolve an issue tomorrow.

This also changes how I measure success. I would track whether consumers can find the product, understand its scope and resolve an issue without a long chain of emails. An agent pilot is a good stress test because it exposes unclear ownership quickly.

The product owner should also hear how the agent is being used. If users repeatedly ask questions the product cannot answer, that is input for the product roadmap. If an agent frequently stops because a field arrives late, the owner can prioritize that issue with the source team. Consumption feedback should improve the product.
